The same individualization occurs in Customer Success: onboarding is left to the assigned person, and both deeper product usage and upsell success depend on personal ability.
As a result, health-score monitoring becomes hollow; churn is discovered only when the customer contacts the company, so early warning signs are missed.

Even if headline numbers still rise, net growth slows and management anxiety spreads. At the stage of aiming for ¥1 billion, the company must define the state in which 'the customer is succeeding' and systematize the process that leads customers there.
Three interlocking factors—'characteristics of the Japanese market,' 'changes in the customer segment,' and 'the wall of individual dependency'—push the company into the 'valley of expansion' (拡大の谷).
The valley arises because the firm continues to drag its early success experiences while a mismatch grows between customer change and the organization's growth speed.
Crossing the valley requires redefining the winning formula (勝ち筋) and elevating it into a reproducible organizational system.

Companies that grow past 500 million yen in sales versus those that stall have three major branching points: (1) redefinition of Who/What, (2) transformation from 'waiting sales' to 'attacking sales', and (3) elimination of individual dependency (属人性の排除).
Who/What redefinition means not being passively carried along by shifts in customer segments, but intentionally causing those customer-segment changes.
Companies that keep growing redesign 'who they serve, what value they provide, and how they deliver it' and thereby establish a second Product-Market Fit (2nd PMF).
Successful firms focus on particular industries or company-size bands, translate their messaging for those segments, and optimize sales methods accordingly.

A drop in win rate can also signal a customer-segment shift; in that case, finely analyze lead data to discover which groups actually want to listen and which of those groups the company can or should actively pursue.

Who/What redefinition is an act of selection and concentration: do not be swayed by a handful of anecdotal cases ('this pattern also exists', 'this customer also exists'); instead plant a few core pillars.

A typical failure mode is fear of missed opportunities that prevents selection and concentration. Spreading too widely causes sales channels to proliferate, proposal patterns to multiply, resources to fragment, and the firm to lose sight of where it should focus.
Therefore it is essential to deliberately 'decide' the pillars that will be pursued.

SmartHR example: after initial success in IT and startups, the company judged that growth would stall in that segment alone. It first defined the product's essential value, then concentrated on food-service, retail and service industries because those firms have high employee turnover and large headcounts—the attributes that make the product's core value most relevant.

The second trial companies must overcome from PMF to ¥10 billion in sales is transforming from “waiting sales” (inbound) to “attacking/proactive sales.” This often emerges naturally as inbound volume changes—e.g., starting outbound or partner/agency sales.

The critical task is identifying the right channel: once the target customer segment (Who) is clear, the most efficient media and channels to reach them become obvious. Whether tele-apo, exhibitions, or web marketing is best depends on the target segment.
Marketing-sales channels are numerous; companies must select and combine those that are most efficient for the chosen customer group.

SmartHR example: after redefining Who/What they simultaneously reset How. Traditional IT-industry methods did not fit restaurants, retail, or services, so they mixed in exhibitions and other channels.

The later trial is eliminating personal dependency (属人性の排除). Stagnating firms typically rely on founders or top salespeople; adding headcount does not produce proportional results (“we hired more salespeople but numbers did not grow”).

Growing companies standardize the sales process so that any representative can achieve a consistent win rate. They also systematize CS (onboarding, health scores, upsell/cross-sell motions) to maximize NRR.
When sales and CS operate as linked systems, ARR grows not only from new logos but also from expansion of existing customers. Timing of this systematization/standardization must not be mistimed.
Before PMF, a company is still in trial-and-error; premature systematization or standardization at that stage actually creates inefficiency.
Systematization should wait until the company has passed the 'phantom PMF phase' and has proven it can compete sufficiently.

Crossing the 'valley of expansion' is decided by selection and concentration: the courage to re-narrow the target, the courage to focus channels rather than spreading them, and the decision to allocate resources to building systems.
Companies that execute those choices can break the 1 billion yen sales wall and then challenge the next 'chasm wall.'
Postponing decisions, clinging to early methods, or scattering resources across too many initiatives leads to stagnation and lost growth opportunities.
The 500 million–1 billion yen revenue range is not merely a waypoint; proving the reproducibility of growth there largely determines the company's future.
Companies that cross the valley of expansion advance with three pillars: redefinition, discernment (the ability to judge what matters), and reproducibility.
Stagnating companies lack at least one of those three pillars and remain stuck.
The decisions made at this branching point determine the subsequent growth story.

Many executives assume that once initial Product-Market Fit (PMF) is achieved, they can simply scale the existing product and go-to-market approach. This is a common and dangerous misconception in B2B growth.

The first companies that adopt a new B2B product are typically innovators and early adopters: they have strong problem awareness, move quickly, tolerate a rough or unfinished product, and can empathize even with relatively vague sales messaging.
Even within the early-adopter segment there is a smaller internal wall. Crossing it requires a further, more precise level of product-market fit rather than mere expansion of the original offering.

2nd PMF is the 're-fit' process that sits between the initial PMF and the chasm (the well-known gap between early adopters and the early majority). It is not optional scaling; it is a distinct stage of re-matching.
Executing 2nd PMF requires a deliberate redefinition of 'Who × What'—who the target customer really is and what value the product must deliver for the next, more demanding layer of buyers.

Without this second fit, companies that looked successful with early innovators often stall before they can reach the mainstream market and larger revenue scale (the book's framing is growth from PMF toward ¥10 billion in sales).
2nd PMF (2ndPMF) is defined as redefining Who / What / How and building the foundation (土台) that allows a company to press the accelerator (アクセルを踏む).
The subsequent content in the book explains the process/engineering of achieving 2nd PMF.

Figure 3-2 illustrates 2nd PMF against the technology adoption lifecycle (diffusion of innovations curve), showing segments such as Early Adapters (アーリーアダプター), Majority (マジョリティ), and Laggards (ラガード) with typical percentages including approximately 2.5%, 13.5%, 34%, and 16%.
The book context is a BtoB Growth Playbook covering five trials companies must overcome to grow from PMF to 10 billion yen in sales (売上100億).

When redefining Who/What/How for 2ndPMF in B2B growth, separate Who/What from How. The first and most important task is appropriate verbalization of 'What': what truly constitutes the value provided to the customer. This is the initial viewpoint that must be grasped.

Once What has been clearly verbalized, use it as the central axis to identify and specify the customer image (Who). Subsequent customers after initial customers are then selected according to a 5-step process.

Sales emphasis differs by customer type/stage (Figure 3-3). Key factors and their relative importance include implementation track record (導入実績, 41%), novelty (新規性, 20%), and case studies/導入事例 (37%, 31%, or 18% depending on the customer group).
The overall framing is part of scaling a B2B company from PMF toward 10 billion yen in revenue, requiring redefinition of Who/What as a core trial.

Step 1 of redefining Who (target customers) is to verbalize value based on quantitative and qualitative analysis of existing customers, starting with grouping past win/loss (受注/失注) reasons: identify which win reasons are reproducible and which loss reasons can be countered.

Among existing customers, identify use cases with notably strong outcomes. Combine quantitative data (ARR contribution, usage depth, upsell rate) with qualitative information (usage context, job title of the introduction decision-maker, how usage expanded inside the company).

Analyze 'successful use cases' as the unit of analysis, not merely 'customers who signed a contract.' This surfaces what value the company is actually delivering and what value it can deliver, so that value can be put into language.

Step 2 is to document target-customer conditions. Do not classify successful customers only by industry or company size; organize them by driver conditions (the situations in which the product’s value is maximized).
This produces a clear redefinition axis: 'Under what customer conditions is product value maximized?'

Step 3 is to redesign personas and set a priority target. Map the conditions of customers with a strong need for the product/service’s value onto attribute axes such as industry/sector and company size.

Draw one scenario that covers not only 'who buys' but also 'who uses and who produces results.' Separate buying-process stakeholders (decision-maker / user / champion) and make bottlenecks explicit so the sales process and success scenario become clear.
The goal image for Step 3 is to be able to state in words which customer group will generate the next ¥500 million.
Step 4 is to make non-targets explicit (have the courage to discard). A trap of the expansion phase is trying to sell to everyone who might possibly buy.

In redefining Who, drawing a clear line on 'customers we will not sell to' is essential. When sales, marketing, and CS share the same target understanding, inefficient deals and implementations decrease and the whole organization’s focus increases.
Step 5 of 2nd PMF is to run a target-hypothesis verification cycle: take the defined Who/What into actual sales, marketing, and CS operations and test it in the field.
Form concrete hypotheses such as “customers who meet these conditions have higher win rates and higher post-implementation usage,” then run them in short AB-test-like cycles.
Redefining Who/What is not a one-time task; it is a process that is continuously polished through verification.
When this feedback loop exists, an organization can move from 1st PMF (person-dependent early success) to a reproducible 2nd PMF.
At the 2nd PMF stage, customer feature requests should not drive “nice-to-have” additions. The work is value translation (価値の翻訳) and product updates built on that translated value.
It is essential to translate, segment by segment, “for whom, what changes, and how.”

When a single clear thread emerges from hypothesis testing, treat it as a product-update axis. If the offering’s value is refined by the update, redefine What, reset Who, and re-run the same verification steps.
The process demands repeated, high-speed verification so that Who/What can be redefined quickly.
2nd PMF is the process of designing, without clinging too tightly to early success, a deeper “who we serve and what value we provide,” then re-fitting the product to that design.

Markets that look similar hide their differences internally. Redesigning Who/What, making choices and concentrating, and following through on what is out of target determines whether a company can cross the valley of expansion and re-accelerate past ¥1 billion in sales.
After redefining who/what (who to deliver what value to) in B2B growth, the next challenge in the expansion phase is How: how to deliberately target and acquire that customer group.
Expansion requires transforming from inbound-centric waiting sales (relying on naturally incoming leads) to a mix that includes outbound, proactive attacking sales.
In the early phase, companies can accumulate revenue from naturally flowing leads via exhibitions, SNS, and referrals/introductions.
Once in the expansion phase, inbound-only channels cannot sustain both the volume (母数) and quality of leads needed.
To fully capture the market's early-adopter layer and enable the next stage of growth, companies must actively set targets and reconstruct their approach (How) rather than remaining passive.
The expansion-phase How discussion focuses on selecting effective measures (施策) and tactical options (打ち手) for customer acquisition after the who/what design is complete.

Premise before considering How (acquisition methods): do not indiscriminately spread tactics widely. Optimal approaches differ completely depending on target: large enterprises, regional SMEs, or ventures/startups. Seriously verify and answer which acquisition channel is optimal.

Many startups start with web ads (e.g., Meta ads) in the early phase because their targets are IT industry or startup companies, which have good affinity with online advertising. Completely different approaches are required when targeting regional companies or large enterprises.

For large-enterprise development, advisory sales is effective: bring in former large-company executives as advisors to secure appointments with key persons, or involve advisors with strong large-enterprise networks to create referral paths. Combine this with holding large conferences/seminars to raise brand awareness while attacking via multiple channels.

For regional-company development, direct sales alone often has limits. Indirect channels that leverage regional networks are extremely important: exhibiting at regional trade shows, partnering with sales agents/distributors, and approaching regional associations and chambers of commerce.

The range of possible tactics (How) is almost entirely determined by the height of the product's LTV. High LTV equals high freedom in How. If LTV is low and no compensating How is visible, first redesign how to raise LTV.

Unit economics is the foundational thinking: what is LTV per customer, and what portion can be invested as CAC (customer acquisition cost). The traditional guideline was LTV:CAC of 3x; recently it is said the ratio should be kept around 5x.

Example: if LTV is 10 million yen, up to 2 million yen per company can be invested in acquisition. At that level the range of tactics expands sharply (trade-show exhibits, large-scale advertising, agent development, own conferences, etc.).
Figure 3.44 in the BtoB Growth Playbook (from PMF to 10 billion yen in sales) is an example of considering lead acquisition channels (リード獲得チャネルの検討例).
Illustrated B2B lead acquisition channels include advisor utilization (顧問活用), exhibitions/trade shows (展示会), introductions from regional banks (地銀紹介), seminars (セミナー), web, and DM/FAX DM.
The example diagram was created by Prib Consulting as a framework for evaluating multiple lead-generation options in B2B growth.

For a B2B business with LTV of 500,000 yen per deal, allowable CAC is typically around 100,000 yen; channels that can acquire a company at under 100,000 yen CAC are extremely limited (referrals, SEO, organic traffic from owned media, inbound from SNS/Web, and PLG/product-led growth).

The optimal 'How' (acquisition tactics and channels) changes with company/product phase even when targeting the same customer segment; distinguish awareness-spreading stages from stages of deeply acquiring specific customers.
Investment channels and KPI design must change by phase; customer acquisition efficiency generally declines as the company advances, so this deterioration should be treated as a given.
Early phase: start small with high-ROI methods such as referrals and small-scale web ads that easily produce positive ROI.
Mid-to-later phases: invest even in less efficient measures in order to acquire customers more broadly and at scale.

A critical judgment is whether the current period is for prioritizing efficiency and reliably generating numbers, or for prioritizing scale even at the cost of efficiency; misjudging this disrupts investment rhythm and causes missed growth opportunities.
Figure 3.5 (図 3.5) in the BtoB Growth Playbook addresses selecting optimal measures (最適な施策) according to a company's current phase (自社のフェーズ).
A key axis in the figure is channel controllability (チャネルのコントロール性), ranging from high (高い) to low (低い), defined as whether the channel can be operationalized or put into regular operation (運用に乗るか).
The figure was created by Prib Consulting (プリブ・コンサルティング作成).

In the initial phase of B2B growth (from PMF toward scale), the highest priority is establishing one overwhelmingly efficient customer-acquisition channel rather than spreading effort across many channels.
Starting with multi-channel expansion disperses limited resources and makes verification of what actually works ambiguous.

Producing reliable results in a single channel typically requires at least about three months of dedicated verification; switching tactics before completing that period prevents identifying why results failed and blocks learning accumulation.
Early-phase mantra: find the channel’s “winning path” (勝ち筋) through single-point concentration (一点集中).

Outbound calling is a common proactive-sales method, but it must not be underestimated. Inbound-trained salespeople told to “go on offense” usually fail without list design, message development, call/approach scripts, and data-accumulation systems, because they are simply unfamiliar with outbound.
Core premise: many venture products are inherently “hard to sell” (売るのが難しい). Outbound difficulty compounds as “hard to sell” × “redefined target” × “message variation by target segment.”
Therefore the critical move is to deliberately stand up a BDR (Business Development Representative) function rather than treating outbound as an ad-hoc extra task.

Outsourcing outbound to a sales agency can be a useful option later, but high-difficulty work given to an external party rarely produces quick results. First build the winning pattern in-house, then outsource.

Once individual channels have been validated, the next stage is cross-channel customer-experience design: treat all touchpoints (exhibitions, web marketing, outbound, etc.) as one coherent “story” rather than independent silos.

Example systematized flow: prospects who showed interest at an exhibition are nurtured with white papers, scored by an MA (marketing-automation) tool, then called by BDRs. This shifts the company from “dependence on individual sales effort” to “automation by scenario.”

In the expansion phase there is no single correct How; effective methods differ by market characteristics and customer attributes. Continuously monitor channel cost-effectiveness, response rates, and post-order LTV, and re-check consistency with the redefined Who × What.

In B2B growth from PMF toward 10 billion yen in sales, sales, marketing, and CS must not operate in silos (縦割り). They should make decisions based on shared KPIs and a common understanding of the customer.
This cross-functional alignment is the key that turns a shift from passive to active operations into a lasting mechanism for sustainable growth (持続的な成長の仕組み).
Figure 3-6 organizes a concrete list of lead-acquisition channels together with the effectiveness of each channel; it is intended as a practical reference.

After Who/What/How is defined, many B2B companies hit the wall of sales reproducibility (営業の再現性): early wins came from founders or a few ace sellers with deep market knowledge, customer-issue understanding, and even product-improvement feedback, using only minimal process.

Founder-led or ace-led personal selling works in the early stage, but expanding headcount does not automatically produce the same results; win rates often drop and companies experience 'we added people but the numbers did not grow.' This is a typical stumble in the 'valley of expansion' (拡大の谷).

Highly personalized selling (custom decks per customer, adaptive talk tracks, reading the room to close) looks effective when observed live, but it is inherently non-reproducible and does not scale beyond the original founders or experienced sellers.
Systematizing sales and creating a repeatable growth model is therefore required once the organization must grow beyond a handful of exceptional individuals.

Star salespeople relying on personal experience and intuition does not scale: tacit knowledge is not converted into explicit, shareable knowledge, so new hires take a long time to become productive. Headcount growth therefore does not produce proportional revenue growth, leaving leadership with the feeling that 'we added people but sales did not grow.'

The first priority when systematizing sales is to optimize the growth model. The right growth model is determined by the combination of product characteristics and target-customer characteristics; companies must correctly diagnose this combination and select the model that actually fits them.
Channel-level analysis is useful, but even more important for efficient growth is answering two questions: 'Which type of growth model do we belong to?' and 'What should we actually benchmark?'

Naive imitation ('that company did X, so we should too') fails because product quality, customer structure, sales motion, decision speed, and the essence of the value proposition differ even when businesses look similar on the surface.

A common failure mode is the indiscriminate adoption of 'The Model' (the specialized, division-of-labor sales system). It is a powerful mechanism for some firms and actively counterproductive for others. The original intent was not merely 'how to create an efficient division of labor' but 'how to design a reproducible growth process that matches your own company structure.'
Therefore the starting point is self-diagnosis: 'Which type do we belong to?' and 'What growth architecture is most suitable for us?'

The authors' framework is the 'Marketing Sales 12MAP' (two-axis matrix). Vertical axis = product characteristics; horizontal axis = customer characteristics. Plotting a company on these axes reveals which growth model is appropriate.

Product characteristics (vertical axis) are classified into at least three types, the first of which is: (1) Replacement / digitization of an existing business—taking an already-understood process (e.g., on-premise expense reimbursement or paper-based workflows) and making it more efficient via cloud or digital delivery.

B2B products/growth models can be classified into three types of value provision: (1) existing-business replacement, (2) new value proposition added to an existing business, and (3) new-category creation.
Existing-business replacement type: analog processes are replaced by digital ones (example: replacing paper business cards with digital card management).

New-value-proposition-to-existing-business type: new functions or perspectives are added to existing mechanisms to deliver new customer value (examples: optimizing customer experience via web-based customer service; optimizing personnel placement via a talent-management system).

New-category-creation type: markets that did not previously exist are created (examples: proposing entirely new mobility infrastructure such as autonomous-driving buses; pioneering new industrial domains such as the space industry).
As a company moves from existing-business replacement toward new-category creation, customer-education costs rise and growth difficulty increases.
A complementary horizontal axis is customer characteristics, divided into four segments: individuals, venture startups, enterprises, and traditional SMBs (legacy industries).
The customer segment a product targets strongly determines the optimal go-to-market approach and the required sales organization.

Figure 3-7 presents the Marketing Sales 12MAP framework from a BtoB Growth Playbook covering the path from PMF (Product-Market Fit) to 10 billion yen in sales and the five trials companies must overcome.

The 12MAP framework organizes B2B marketing and sales approaches along two primary value types: (1) replacement of existing business via efficiency gains, and (2) new value propositions to existing businesses that raise added value and WTP (willingness to pay).
One cluster of tactics appeals to understandability, division-of-labor efficiency, and status-quo bias, using a close-following marketing-sales system that stays close to the customer.
Another cluster focuses on usage development and experiential value: narrowing the target, leveraging mobilizers, and piercing deeply into that segment.
A further tactic is to conquer internal human networks (社内人脈) inside the customer organization.
Advanced-worldview tactics include igniting groups of innovators and co-creating the current of the times together with industry-transformation leaders.
List sales is listed as a distinct approach within the map.
A resource-efficiency dimension (labeled 1D) emphasizes minimizing CAC (customer acquisition cost) while maximizing the use of external resources.
The diagram is attributed to Leap Consulting (リブ・コンサルティング) as original material.
The two axes of BtoB growth combine to produce the Marketing Sales 12MAP, a grid of 12 squares, each with its own optimal growth model.

1-B type (replacement of existing business × venture/startup) is best served by a division-of-labor efficiency organization known as The Model. Because unit prices are not high, the company must efficiently acquire a large number of customers; early targets (ventures and startups) also have high IT literacy. The effective model is therefore web-marketing-centered mass lead generation, followed by collaboration among Inside Sales, Field Sales, and Customer Success to convert leads into orders. Many startups launch from this 1-B square.

2-C type (new value proposition to existing business × enterprise) requires a completely different approach: not volume-chasing The Model, but an ABM-style strategy of strategically conquering one account at a time. Enterprise buying involves multiple departments and consensus-building, so Challenger-Sales-style strategic selling is required.
The contrast between 1-B and 2-C produces entirely different organization designs, talent requirements, skill sets, and management styles.
A company does not remain in the same square of the 12MAP. As business phase and customer base change, the company must deliberately move to a different fighting square.

Example: SmartHR began in the venture-centric 1-B square, growing via web marketing; it later entered the enterprise (2-C) market, stood up a dedicated enterprise sales organization, and developed customers with an entirely different logic, producing results.

Therefore the first tasks are to identify which square the company currently occupies and to decide which square it will next target. When the fighting square changes, required talent, go-to-market methods, and organization design all change at once. Understanding that shift and designing the growth architecture around it is the key to making growth reproducible.
There is no single correct growth model. What matters is understanding one’s own product and customer structure and continuously selecting the fighting style that fits the current phase.
After understanding the 12MAP structure, a company should draw an original growth model suited to itself; that is the path described.
The next critical topic after that structure is the systematization of sales (営業) and success (サクセス / customer success).
Systematizing sales and success is what enables a company to go beyond 2nd PMF and realize sustainable growth.
The surrounding book framing is a B2B growth playbook on the five trials a company must overcome from PMF to 10 billion yen in sales.

When modeling/standardizing a B2B sales process, key elements that must be standardized one by one include: required hearing/discovery confirmation items, demo scenarios that must be covered, proposal document structure, and talking points for competitor comparisons. This ensures anyone can deliver a consistent quality of engagement.

Sales process standardization is not merely unifying slides or materials. It means designing the sales conversation itself and explicitly documenting, for each stage: what must be confirmed, what must be delivered/handed over, and how far the deal must have progressed before it can advance to the next stage.
Putting this designed process in place removes sales from being personal art (属人芸 / individual heroics) and raises the reproducibility of growth.

Once the sales process is standardized, metrics become visible and trackable at the team level: stage-to-stage conversion rates, average sales-cycle length, win rate, and loss reasons. Tracking these as a team makes bottlenecks obvious.

In early, person-dependent sales, loss reasons stay only in the individual salesperson’s head and are never reused. With a designed process, causes become diagnosable (e.g., “did not advance because required hearing items were missed” or “lost at proposal because non-functional requirements were never addressed”).

Standardizing B2B sales is not merely creating standard sales materials; it requires assembling a full set of reproducible 'weapons' so any sales member can produce results: (1) customer-type judgment, (2) type-specific Who/What details, (3) concrete scenario talk examples, (4) closing talk, (5) competitive comparison table, and (6) internal-approval (escalation) material format.

Customer-type judgment uses the defined Who/What to create branching criteria that identify the prospect type. Identification can occur during the meeting via hearing or earlier at the inside-sales stage, turning random 'whatever comes' meetings into targeted, intended deals.

Type-specific Who/What documentation goes beyond simple Who/What labels. It organizes concrete use cases, which appeals actually land, which product features most readily create perceived value, and type-specific competitors plus countermeasures. This lets the salesperson know exactly what must be covered in the meeting.

Scenario-talk construction first maps each slide's role in the overall flow and its goal/appeal message so the salesperson can picture how to step the customer's psychology forward. Those messages are then written onto each page of the deck together with sample talk. Because people speak differently, the focus is on the non-negotiable 'must-cover' points per slide so the core message never drifts even if delivery style varies.

Closing talk is a distinct, indispensable layer. Once a company moves from reactive to proactive selling, the belief that 'if we just communicate the right things the deal will close' is revealed as an illusion; without a proper close, surprisingly few deals actually close.
When these elements make causes of success and failure visible, improvements can be accumulated as organizational knowledge rather than remaining individual tacit skill.

In B2B sales scaling (from PMF toward large revenue), even test-closing and closing talk tracks must be templated so the organization finishes with a repeatable “decisive sales” (決め切る営業) playbook rather than ad-hoc conversations.

Competitive comparison tables are core input content every sales member should internalize: what each competitor claims, where their strengths lie, and the seller’s own advantages and disadvantages versus those competitors, then mapped onto the customer’s actual needs.
Competitive exclusion is frequently left as tacit, artisan-style talk owned by veteran sellers; it must instead be standardized into reusable templates so the whole team can execute it consistently.
Sales-meeting (商談) processes are often templated, yet the supporting “weapons” required to actually close—especially internal-approval (上申) document formats—are rarely created.

Direct access to the Right Man / decision-maker (RM) during evaluation is uncommon; most opportunities travel through an internal approval chain and are frequently postponed or killed at that stage with an NG from a superior.

The person who sat in the sales meeting and that person’s boss occupy different positions, carry different responsibilities, and own different scopes of authority; therefore the seller must supply explanation materials that can independently persuade the superior.
Without materials capable of convincing the approver’s boss, the seller cannot claim to be winning deals in a targeted, repeatable way (see accompanying figures 3-8 and 3-9).
Figure 3-8 (営業プロセスの見える化①) presents a framework for visualizing the B2B sales process, created by Prim Consulting.
Sales process visualization begins with identifying Who * What as the core pairing of target customer and offering.
The framework uses 営業シナリオ (sales scenarios) to map the overall process flow.
A key step is knowing the flow of the process together with 具体的な手法 (specific techniques/methods) for selling to a given customer type (このタイプに売るための).
A more detailed layer focuses on より具体的な流れと伝え方を知る (knowing a more concrete flow and how to communicate/convey the message).
The visualization distinguishes a high-level Who * What view from a more operational view that specifies Who, the detailed sequence, and What (the communication of the offering).

In the B2B growth stage after product-market fit (PMF) toward 10 billion yen in sales, companies need an internal sales support system so that expanding sales headcount does not stall on long time-to-productivity.

The most critical mechanism is internal education / onboarding. Success or failure of onboarding dramatically shortens time-to-productivity and substantially changes retention rates; supporting the initial ramp-up is therefore extremely important.

Onboarding systematization follows five steps (Figure 3-10): (1) For the target organizational structure, define the talent profile to be developed, then decompose required skills and stances into concrete elements. (2) Define acquisition steps: set phased milestones and clarify the required level of each element at every step. (3) Define how each step is climbed: link milestones to roles, work, and positions so they form a gradual career path. (4) Design content and opportunities matched to the purpose and characteristics of the elements needed at each step. (5) Produce the actual onboarding content according to the overall designed picture.

Going through sales systematization (仕組み化) steps clarifies talent requirements (人材要件), lowers hiring difficulty (採用難易度), raises training reproducibility (育成の再現性), and increases the number of immediately productive hires (即戦力化人材).

Input content (インプットコンテンツ) covers prerequisite knowledge for job acquisition, portable skills (ポータブルスキル), and customer understanding (顧客理解) needed to advance sales conversations; without correctly grasping this knowledge, practical execution is impossible, so tests are used to verify understanding.
After knowledge input, practical training checks whether sales scenario talks (営業シナリオプトーク) can be delivered appropriately, confirmed through role-playing (ロールプレイング).
These elements are designed as a curriculum that also specifies how new hires should spend their first month after joining.
Sales systematization and reproducibility-building (再現性づくり) may appear mundane, but companies that cannot overcome this stage will see growth stall no matter how much they increase headcount.
Companies that standardize processes and convert knowledge into explicit knowledge (ナレッジを形式知化) lower hiring and training difficulty so that sales grow in proportion to organizational scale.
To cross the valley of expansion (拡大の谷), it is essential to eliminate individual dependence in sales (営業の属人性を排除) and create a system in which whoever sells can produce consistent results.
After sales processes are systematized, the next priority in B2B growth (post-PMF toward 10B yen revenue) is implementing post-onboarding customer support through Customer Success (CS).

A frequent company complaint is that new-logo acquisition is growing while overall revenue accumulation remains sluggish: monthly new contracts are won, yet cancellations and usage contraction keep net expansion smaller than expected, flattening the growth curve.
The root cause is typically the absence of a functioning CS mechanism/organization; without it, even strong new-business results fail to compound into stacked recurring revenue.
In subscription models, growth is designed on the assumption that contracts continue, so churn rate is equally or more important than new-contract volume.
A dedicated Success organization is required to prevent the 'sales do not accumulate' outcome that occurs when only acquisition is optimized.
In SaaS, once churn exceeds a certain level it cancels out stacked revenue growth, so net sales stop compounding even if new logos are added.

Churn rate sets the upper bound of long-term growth: only companies at ~10% churn or below keep growing after 20 years; 15–20% churn yields modest growth for 10–20 years then near-zero; 25–35% churn yields almost no growth after 10 years (Sakuma Ko / former Userbase co-CEO, note article on SaaS churn).
In the “valley of expansion” stage, headline numbers can look like growth while actual net-new revenue is tiny; that is why this stage requires a frontal attack on churn prevention and retention.

The first retention bottleneck is customer onboarding: whether a newly implemented customer can stand up smoothly right after go-live largely determines subsequent continuation rates (the mechanism is analogous to internal sales-team onboarding).
Person-dependent, ad-hoc implementation support produces large variance between successful and failed customers and therefore inflates overall churn.
Standardizing the onboarding process so every customer is guaranteed to experience tangible value within a defined time window can cut churn substantially.
Many SaaS firms treat “the first 90 days” as decisive because the quality of the initial value experience governs multi-year contract retention.
The dual essence of Customer Success is churn prevention plus systematic upsell/cross-sell (more seats, additional departments, plan upgrades, new modules).
Growth speed changes when CS designs expansion paths and can show the customer a clear “what comes next” roadmap rather than leaving expansion to one-off sales conversations.

Ad-hoc sales-led upsell/cross-sell can produce some results but is not sustainable; companies must mechanize who proposes what, at which timing, and in which scenario so expansion becomes reproducible.
A practical pattern is to present customers who have already reached a success state with explicit branching paths for further expansion (illustrated in the book’s Figure 3-11).
When defining customers, do not rely on metrics/indicators; instead, gain insight into which scenario you are on and take action accordingly.
Figure 3-11 is an example of defining customers, involving embedding into business workflows and roles such as the person in charge for the next period.
Source of the figure: created by Prib Consulting.
To achieve a customer's ideal state, Customer Success (CS) must use both human resources and technology to sort required actions, and deciding what not to do is extremely important.

To raise reproducibility of customer success, prepare an overall map and a time-series flow: summarize what can happen at each customer phase and the corresponding actions, and document the step-up path to success for a focused customer. This lets teams see whether the customer is on-scenario or off-scenario, whether there is upsell/cross-sell potential, and whether there is churn risk.

Data from CS activities should be treated as numbers that reflect customers' deep psychology and behavior. Elevating CS to a strategic function requires metric-based management, but the metrics are only the surface of that deeper reality.

NRR (Net Revenue Retention) is a representative outcome metric. It shows the growth rate of existing-customer revenue including upsell and cross-sell. NRR below 100% means existing-customer revenue is net declining and the foundation of growth is shaking. NRR above 100% means ARR grows naturally from existing-customer expansion alone.

Health-score design is essential for raising NRR. Combine quantitative data (login frequency, feature utilization rate) with qualitative information to visualize customer health, and build a mechanism that alerts immediately on abnormal values. This enables matching which metrics actually drive NRR and which steps customers take toward upsell/cross-sell.

If the metrics you want to improve are not rising, that is evidence that CS activities are not following the intended scenario. This makes it possible to detect churn signs early and intervene proactively.

CS must not merely act as a support window that receives inquiries. It must actively monitor customer health using both quantitative metrics and qualitative information, then connect that monitoring to usage promotion and additional proposals.

Many companies postpone CS because growth still looks healthy while sales is generating numbers. Without CS, growth will soon plateau. Strengthening the success organization itself is the branching point that determines whether a company can cross the 'valley of expansion'.
Successful companies position CS as a growth driver rather than a mere support window: they standardize onboarding and put churn-prevention mechanisms in place.
To sustain B2B growth after PMF, companies should maintain NRR (Net Revenue Retention) of 100% or higher on an ongoing basis so revenue can compound without relying only on new logos.
After customers are onboarded and settled (定着), expansion must be deliberately designed and executed organizationally through upsell and cross-sell motions rather than left to chance.

Customer Success (CS) should own post-onboarding expansion (upsell/cross-sell) as well as retention; when CS does this, sales can accumulate even without new contracts and growth becomes more sustainable.

Failing companies treat CS like a “customer consultation / support desk” and limit it to reactive support. The result is unimproved churn, missed expansion opportunities, and eventual limits to new-logo-dependent growth.
Core contrast: CS as a growth engine (retention + designed expansion, NRR ≥ 100%) vs. CS as a helpdesk (support-only, high dependence on new acquisition).

In the expansion phase of B2B growth (after defining targets and building sales/customer success), partner sales becomes necessary to reach customer segments that direct sales cannot easily access, such as regional SMEs, legacy industries, and certain enterprise departments.
Partner sales means opening a market together with third parties who already have established routes and relationships in the target domain.

Two critical cautions when launching partner sales: (1) success or failure is largely determined by who you partner with (affinity/compatibility), not merely brand name; (2) it is not a single tactic but an initiative closer to launching a new business, requiring a 2–3 year time horizon of design, verification, and expansion.
Teams often become overly excited by a partner’s name value once a deal is signed; this is a common trap because name recognition alone does not guarantee results.
In B2B growth from product-market fit (PMF) toward large-scale revenue (e.g., ¥10 billion), many partner-sales programs fail in practice rather than succeeding as hoped.
The author states that the reality is that numerous partner-sales efforts are not going well (illustrated by Figure 3-12).

In B2B growth after product-market fit (PMF), vendors often assume sales will scale in proportion to the number of channel partners (代理店); the ideal model treats each additional agent as additive capacity that moves product for the vendor.
Figure 3-12 contrasts that ideal with reality: most agents do not actually act or sell (ほとんどの代理店は動かない), so output does not grow with headcount of partners.
The gap between hoped-for partner motion and actual partner inaction is framed as a core trial companies must overcome on the path from PMF to ¥10 billion in sales.

The diagram labels a vendor (ベンダー) feeding four agents in the ideal case versus a reality in which the majority of agents remain idle, underscoring that partner count is a poor proxy for partner productivity.
When selecting B2B partners after PMF, expecting only the partner’s rich customer assets or wide sales-channel coverage is insufficient for growth; the partnership often still fails.

Construction-industry wallet structure is typically allocated per job site, and purchases used on-site are decided by the site supervisor; therefore a partner with frequent route-sales access to site supervisors looks theoretically ideal.

Case: a construction-DX SaaS that already had PMF, inbound traction, and direct-sales customers partnered with a nationwide construction-materials distributor that had branches and site-supervisor relationships. After six months of product and sales-method training, monthly partner-sourced opportunities remained only single- or low-double-digit.

Two core reasons the partnership failed despite clear ICP, PMF product, and taught selling method: (1) poor affinity with the partner’s salespeople and (2) absence of a compelling “reason to sell” for those salespeople.

Affinity failure: the partner’s salespeople historically sold physical construction materials (“mono-uri”) via existing routes and inbound phone orders from site supervisors; asking them to create demand for a novel IT/SaaS product was far too high-difficulty.

Motivation / “reason-to-sell” failure: the commercial model shared recurring SaaS revenue, which was attractive to the partner’s executives and helped close the partnership, yet it did not create sufficient day-to-day motivation for the individual salespeople who actually had to sell.

Even when target-company resolution is high, the product has achieved PMF, and the selling method has been explained, partner motion can still be near-zero if salesperson affinity and personal selling motivation are missing.

Partner sales often fail not because of weak executive-level alliances, but because field salespeople have no personal motivation to sell the partner product. Management may understand the strategic value of a partnership, but the people who actually meet customers are frontline sales reps.

A common structural mismatch: salespeople face high difficulty selling an unfamiliar product, while their evaluation system (e.g., monthly gross-profit targets) makes a small revenue-share (only tens of thousands of yen per month) not worth the time and effort.

The core design principle for partner sales is not “partner with the company” but “create a structure that makes the partner’s field sales team actually move.” Without a clear “reason to sell” for those reps, even a well-written alliance contract will not generate deals.
Partner selection should prioritize affinity (噛み合わせ / 親和性) rather than merely being in the same industry. Affinity should be assessed on three dimensions.

Customer-structure affinity: Check whether the partner’s customers (industry, company size, job hierarchy) match your target customer and target buyer layer. Same industry is not enough; the partner must actually have access to the decision-makers you need.

Sales-motion affinity: The partner’s selling style must fit how your product is sold. Asking a company that sells physical goods to sell an intangible SaaS product typically creates high difficulty and heavy education cost for their salespeople.

Incentive affinity: The partner’s sales KPIs and compensation must align with the return from selling your product. If the partner evaluates salespeople on monthly gross profit, a purely stock/recurring-revenue share will not motivate the field; monthly incentives or immediate rewards are required.

Partner sales functions only when three points of affinity are aligned; more important than partner company size or brand is whether the sales team's motivation structure matches your own company—selection should focus on this fit.
Agree with partner-company management to specially incorporate partner-related activities into compensation systems and evaluations, and operate those systems.
Partner sales starts at the moment the contract is signed; the 2–3 years from launch to scale must be intentionally designed in stages.

Phase 1 (Design period, ~0–6 months): Clarify with the partner who to sell to and how among the partner’s customers; jointly narrow to one shared use case and co-create BHAA–FAQ–HRT templates; also set up incentive mechanisms and lead-sharing rules. Creating an operational playbook the field can actually use is more important than the contract itself.

Phase 2 (Verification period, ~6–18 months): Run joint sales with a small number of partner salespeople; monitor customer reactions, opportunity rates, and close rates; review biweekly, monthly, and quarterly to visualize which customers and which talk tracks resonate. Start with a toss-up model (partner and own sales accompany each other) rather than a full-close model (partner completes independently).

Phase 3 (Expansion period, ~18–36 months): Once success cases and knowledge have accumulated, strengthen education, compensation, and co-hosted marketing so partners can operate independently. Effective tactics include success-case sharing sessions, joint monitoring systems, and building a partner program. At this stage, 20–30% of deal sources can come via partners.
Preparation before launch accounts for 80% of partner-sales success; mechanisms to prevent failure must be built in advance.
Three mechanisms that substantially lower the failure rate of B2B partner sales: (1) enablement design, (2) visualization of data and KPIs, and (3) sharing of success models.

Enablement design: Partners need far more education than expected before they can understand and sell a product. Beyond manuals and videos, continuously provide live deal role-plays, implementation-case sharing sessions, and a dedicated Q&A channel. Stationing one of your own employees at the partner firm can also be effective.

Data and KPI visualization: Build a single dashboard that tracks how many opportunities partners toss up and which of those close. Running partner activity on data rather than gut feel or personal relationships enables the right support and the right compensation design.

Success-model sharing: Design CS-team collaboration so partners can support not only the sale but also post-implementation customer outcomes. When partners themselves perform onboarding, standardize the onboarding playbook and the success metrics they will be measured against.

Partner sales is not a simple “sign the contract and revenue appears” machine. Success hinges on whether you can engineer a structure that gives the partner’s front-line salespeople a genuine reason to sell. That requires selecting highly compatible partners, running joint experiments over a 2–3 year horizon, and treating education, compensation, and data as an inseparable trinity.

Money Forward example: To win cloud-accounting adoption they first targeted Japan’s tax-accountant (zeirishi) network. They deliberately shipped a “legacy” UI that accounting professionals already found familiar, turning those professionals into enthusiastic partners and thereby driving nationwide penetration.

Safie example: For a hardware-plus-SaaS cloud-camera product they obsessed over “hands-off” simplicity—literally “plug in power and it works.” Removing every configuration burden made the offering trivial both for end users and for the partners who sell it, producing explosive growth.

Partners in B2B growth are not merely sales channels; they are another team that co-creates the business. Companies that steadily build these processes—though it takes time—can open markets that direct sales cannot reach and achieve reproducible expansion (再現性ある拡張).

Around ARR of about 500 million yen, many companies hit the first serious stall called the Valley of Expansion (拡大の谷). Typical symptoms: new contracts are still won but net ARR does not grow as expected; adding salespeople does not produce proportional results; work becomes highly person-dependent so new hires fail to raise performance.
This stall is not accidental. It is a structural challenge common to Japanese B2B startups.

To cross the Valley of Expansion, first redefine Who / What / How and fully establish a 2nd PMF within the early-adopter layer. Do not cling to the initial success story; redesign messaging and the sales process for the next core customer.

Second, systematize sales and customer success (CS) so the company moves from person-dependence (属人性) to reproducibility. Standardize processes so that whoever owns the account can produce results; ARR then compounds from both new logos and existing customers.
When Who/What/How, 2nd PMF, and systematized sales/CS are in place, the organization has enough depth to withstand further growth.

Self-check questions: Are you overly dependent on new bookings, and does net increase still accumulate stably after churn? Have you defined the next target customer for 2nd PMF, the value you offer them, and which channels you will use for offensive sales?
BtoB growth after PMF includes a stage called the valley of expansion (拡大の谷). If a company cannot cross it, stagnation becomes the normal state rather than a temporary dip.

Sales win rate must not depend on a few ace reps, the founder, or a minimal set of leftover standard sales materials. The process has to be systematized so that whoever owns the deal can produce comparable results.
Customer Success (CS) must not be treated as a mere support window. It needs mechanisms for retention (定着) and upsell, with a target of NRR (Net Revenue Retention) of 100% or higher.
Pausing at this stage to inspect and rebuild the company’s structure is not only a fix for the valley; it can become the preparation phase for a much larger leap.
The practical work to cross the valley: redefine the target, deliberately discard non-targets, build a reproducible sales and customer-success playbook (型), and establish a growth model.
That groundwork becomes the foothold for breaking through ARR of 10 oku yen (ARR 10億円) and then challenging the next barrier, the chasm wall (キャズムの壁).
The decisive diagnostic question is: Is your company’s growth already a reproducible structure? How the company answers that question determines whether it can get out of the valley of expansion.
Special Interview 02 in the BtoB Growth Playbook features Masanobu Takeda, Director, Executive Officer and Business Segment COO of Money Forward Inc.

Takeda's career: 2001 planning and sales at an internet advertising agency; 2003 joined Macromill and became director in 2008, overseeing business divisions and leading business strategy, HR strategy, corporate integration, and new business development; 2012 joined Iole as Director and Head of Corporate Planning; 2016 Director and CFO of Clavis; 2017 joined the Money Forward Group.
Money Forward Inc. was established in May 2012 as a platform company aiming to solve money-related issues for all people.
Company mission: 「お金を前へ。人生をもっと前へ。」 (Move money forward. Move life further forward.)
Services include the personal money visualization service Money Forward ME, the business back-office SaaS Money Forward Cloud, and co-creation businesses with financial institutions.
Money Forward listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange Mothers market (now Growth) in 2017 and moved to the First Section (now Prime) in 2021.

B2B startups aiming from PMF to ¥10 billion in sales typically face five sequential walls: (1) Phantom/illusory PMF (幻のPMF), (2) Valley of expansion (拡大の谷), (3) Chasm wall (キャズムの壁), (4) Multi-product swamp (マルチプロダクトの沼), and (5) Market limits and hegemony struggle (市場の限界と覇権争い).
Money Forward experienced all five walls; PMF-stage struggles and rapid-growth walls arrived simultaneously around November 2017 when Takeda joined.
Early Money Forward products were feature-incomplete versus competitors’ on-premise (install-type) software, so they lacked true market fit in the sense of fully substituting incumbents.
Instead of Product-Led Growth (PLG), the company used a “Vision-Led Growth” approach—selling the long-term vision rather than current product completeness.

Overcoming the Valley of Expansion is framed as shifting the organization from a “rule-of-man” (人治国家) state to a “rule-of-law” (法治国家) state so growth can be systematized rather than founder-dependent.

In Money Forward's early stage, all members (including sales) consistently told the founding story, mission ('お金を前へ。人生をもっと前へ。' / 'Move money forward. Move life further forward.'), and vision of a money platform—even showing in-development features—to SMEs and accounting firms. This created the expectation that 'with Money Forward, a better future is possible,' which was the main reason they gained support before the product fully caught up.
Presenting a large-scale 'vision' (grand conception) won trust and raised expectations among partners, buying time to rush development so reality could catch up to the promise.
After the initial vision-driven phase, as revenue grew they encountered the '拡大の谷' (Valley of Expansion).
Around Nov 2017–Nov 2018 (SaaS phase), the company still operated as a '人治国家的な組織' (rule-of-man organization): sales came from strong vision-telling individuals acting like '個人商店' (independent shops).
Once the innovator layer had been fully penetrated, individual high activity volume alone no longer produced results.

Fairness problems existed: uniform targets were set despite salespeople having different territories and account sizes, because data/facts were not shared transparently and the overall strategy function was weak.

They shifted to a '法治国家的な組織' (rule-of-law organization based on data and systems) by launching BizOps-like specialist teams and a business-strategy function. This removed bottlenecks from personal success stories and inefficient processes and enabled fact-based, fair operations.
To cross the 'キャズムの壁' (chasm), they deliberately adopted an omnidirectional distribution strategy from the start; this later became a competitive MOAT.
After organizational chaos, B2B SaaS growth next hits the 'chasm wall': innovators are saturated and expansion must reach regional markets and the majority layer.

Money Forward pursued an all-around GTM from the start—not only web marketing/direct sales, but reseller partnerships with accounting firms, regional office expansion, and early alliances with financial institutions and chambers of commerce.

Standard early-stage SaaS playbook is refined web marketing plus a minimal sales org; Money Forward did the opposite. Completing the harder, lower-probability path became their first MOAT (competitive advantage).

Web marketing mainly acquires high-IT-literacy managers. Accounting-firm partners reach traditional SMEs that do not yet use cloud systems; regional and industry innovators among those clients acted as evangelists and pulled the product into the majority.

Positioning vs. freee: freee marketed 'accounting software you can use without knowing bookkeeping' (disrupting existing frameworks). Money Forward positioned as 'next-generation accounting software for accounting professionals.' GTM therefore diverged: freee via web for high-literacy firms; Money Forward via partner sales including regional markets.
The back-office SaaS originated from proposals by accounting-firm professionals, so product strategy optimized for 'how easy is this cloud service for accounting-firm professionals.'

UI/UX choice: typical cloud software was mouse-optimized; Money Forward deliberately optimized keyboard workflows (Enter, Tab) matching traditional accounting software so experts' familiar operations created a distinct edge for accounting firms.

Product expansion at this B2B SaaS company began organically by solving adjacent customer pains rather than from a pre-planned compound strategy: cloud accounting alone was insufficient if invoicing stayed paper-based and payroll linkage was missing, so products naturally spread around accounting as the team stayed close to operational issues.

Early product growth felt similar to incremental feature additions at other firms, with the lineup expanding around the core accounting workflow rather than as a deliberate multi-product vision from day one.

From 2020 to 2021 the company concentrated on rapidly releasing many products aimed at mid-sized enterprises because (1) growth in the original sole-proprietor/SMB market was slowing with scale, (2) early customers were themselves scaling and generating new needs, and (3) a high medium-to-long-term growth rate had to be maintained.

Discontinuous growth required fundamental organizational and strategic change: in 2019 a production-sales-integrated (製販一体) virtual-company system was introduced so that one business-company leader could oversee the entire back-office SaaS business.

To ship a large number of products in a short window, a development hub was established in Vietnam for joint development with Japan—an unconventional, high-risk decision given that Japanese business systems are culturally and procedurally complex and the Vietnamese engineers lacked local domain knowledge.
Building the Vietnam development capability later proved to be a second competitive moat (MOAT), enabling the mid-market product lineup that supported the next phase of growth.
Releasing product groups at explosive speed can help maintain growth rates after achieving product-market fit in B2B SaaS.

Sales organizations should be adapted to product and customer segments: a dedicated Mid-Market Sales Force can be spun out independently when releasing products for mid-sized companies, with formations changed flexibly according to scale and domain.

Sustaining mid-to-long-term growth often requires succeeding at high-difficulty, large-scale challenges. Building a MOAT (competitive moat) typically demands following through on decisions that would normally be viewed as abnormal or impossible.
Growth beyond 10 billion yen in revenue depends on a unique winning path (storyline) plus human capability that goes beyond pure rationality.

Do not overly fixate on a round revenue milestone such as 10 billion yen itself. When TAM (Total Addressable Market) is very large, executing what must be done well allows the company to grow with the market.
A more important capability shift is improved management capability that enables planning by backcasting from 5–10 years ahead rather than only near-term targets.
Publicly committing to a distant goal (e.g., 100 billion yen in FY28, announced nearly five years earlier in FY23) makes reverse-engineered near-term investments and moves visible and actionable.

Advice for growth-oriented executives: discover an original path or storyline. In large markets still dominated by historic incumbents (e.g., ERP), SaaS vendors have not fully captured share; the key is how to compete, not merely that a market and trend exist.

Create a clear difference versus others inside a large market by drawing a distinctive storyline—examples include SmartHR creating a new market segment within HR, and LayerX expanding around expense management as an axis. Thoroughly thinking through this differentiation is essential.
In the coming era of B2B growth (from PMF toward 10 billion yen and beyond), rational strategy alone is insufficient; 'person-to-person realization/execution power' (人対人の実現力) becomes more important.
Scaling sales to 10 billion or 30 billion yen makes M&A unavoidable.
M&A success requires more than strategic theory: organizations must fuse people with people, and technology must be used to create differentiation.
Human creativity (クリエイティビティ) and combining/binding power (結合力) are indispensable for discontinuous (non-linear) growth.

After overcoming the 'valley of expansion' (拡大の谷), a B2B company regained growth momentum by redefining its target customers, standardizing the product introduction/onboarding process, and strengthening collaboration between sales and customer success (CS) teams.
These initiatives established a so-called '2nd PMF' (second Product-Market Fit) after initial product-market fit.
With 2nd PMF in place, adoption expanded across multiple industries and ARR (Annual Recurring Revenue) surpassed 1 billion yen (10億円).
Greater market recognition followed, including increased media coverage and more inbound requests to hear the company's story or lessons.
At exhibitions, large-enterprise representatives began approaching proactively with business cards, indicating readiness for the enterprise segment.
Leadership then switched the sales strategy to an 'enterprise shift' (エンタープライズシフト) to pursue the enterprise market.
The narrative frames a common post-initial-growth challenge: the 'ceiling becoming visible' and stronger headwinds facing top management before the next scaling phase.

In B2B scaling after PMF, growth can stall even as deal volume rises: enterprise opportunities often fail to progress because customer internal coordination takes too long, causing fade-outs after repeated proposals.
Enterprise contract wins do not restore prior growth speed; implementation itself may slip by six months to a full year, visibly eroding the tempo that previously supported expansion.
A split often appears between an SMB/mid-market team that continues to stack numbers and an enterprise team targeting large accounts that produces little result.
Hiring expensive, experienced enterprise sellers and converting high-performing SMB reps into enterprise roles frequently fails to deliver expected outcomes in the short term.

Internal resistance then grows: colleagues question whether enterprise pursuit is the right move now versus first winning decisively in the mid-market, and pressure on the enterprise unit intensifies.

The episode frames the enterprise-market expansion barrier as unexpectedly thick, illustrating one of the sequential trials companies face when trying to grow from product-market fit toward large-scale (e.g., 10-billion-yen) revenue.
In Japanese B2B SaaS/growth, many companies hit the so-called "chasm wall" (キャズムの壁) in the ARR range of roughly 1–2 billion yen (ARR10億〜20億円).
The chasm is the large discontinuity in adoption between innovators/early adopters and the early majority, as described in Everett M. Rogers' Innovator Theory (イノベーター理論 / Diffusion of Innovations).

Although the chasm is theoretically a worldwide phenomenon, in the Japanese market it appears particularly early and stands thicker, due to Japan's special circumstances and the limits of domestic market size.

Japanese B2B startups often stall at ¥1–2 billion in revenue because cultural, institutional, IT-literacy, and market-size factors raise the hurdle from early adopters to the early majority (the chasm).

Japan’s ‘try-first’ culture is weak compared with the U.S.: American firms often let field teams or department heads adopt new tools and evaluate them in use, while Japanese firms prefer to confirm other companies’ case studies before considering a trial, slowing expansion into the early majority.

Large Japanese enterprises have complex decision processes involving IT, audit, legal, and corporate planning, which lengthens time-to-adoption and produces frequent ‘PoC止まり’ (proof-of-concept that never converts to a paid contract).
Institutional barriers therefore make the leap from early adopters to early majority structurally harder in Japan.

IT literacy is highly uneven: large firms have dedicated IT staff, but many mid-size and SMB firms lack a dedicated owner, raising the psychological barrier to SaaS and thinning the early-adopter layer so the growth curve hits a ceiling sooner.
Because that ‘runway’ of early adopters is shorter than overseas, Japanese startups confront the chasm earlier in their trajectory.

Market size also shifts where the chasm appears: focusing only on SMB hits a ceiling quickly, so companies must enter the enterprise segment earlier to keep growing; in a large market SMB concentration can still reach meaningful scale, but in a niche market enterprise entry is unavoidable.
The combination of weak trial culture, complex approvals, IT-literacy gaps, and smaller addressable SMB pools explains why Japanese startups feel stagnation at the ¥10–20 billion sales stage.

The 'chasm wall' (キャズムの壁) in B2B growth is not merely the phenomenon that expanding customer count becomes harder; it is being confronted with the reality that 'with the current market and customer approach alone, further rapid growth cannot be expected.'
Growing companies that continue scaling recognize this wall head-on and determine the market they treat as their core fortress (本丸とする市場).
Strategic choices at the chasm: concentrate on SMB for long-term accumulation (長期積み上げ), step into enterprise, or strategically combine both as dual engines (両輪).
The chasm wall is not a mere hurdle but a forcing question of 'how to prepare/seed the next growth engine' (次の成長エンジンをどう仕込むか).
Context: BtoB Growth Playbook covering the five trials companies must overcome from PMF (product-market fit) to 10 billion yen in sales.

Japanese startups aiming for 1–2 billion yen in sales often adopt an “SMB concentration strategy” because SMBs have relatively fast decision-making and lower initial adoption barriers than large enterprises, making them suitable for accumulating revenue from the early founding stage.

SMB sales approaches tend to be simple: deals frequently close after direct conversations with executives or frontline staff, and leads can be acquired efficiently through trade shows and online advertising, making a “start with SMB first” strategy a natural choice.
Until the 2000s, Japanese startups were predominantly B2C-focused; B2B—especially large-enterprise business—was monopolized by SIers, leaving little room for startups to enter.
Early SaaS players that emerged at the dawn of SaaS in Japan therefore targeted SMEs, replacing existing paper, FAX, and Excel-based workflows.

A core strategic fork for Japanese B2B startups after PMF is whether to deepen the SMB market or attempt the enterprise market; crossing that wall is presented as one of the five trials on the path from PMF to 10 billion yen in sales.

Successful B2B SaaS companies such as freee and Money Forward achieved rapid growth in accounting and HR by first building a strong foothold in the SMB market, proving to later startups that SMB concentration is a natural strategy.

SMB market strengths include fast adoption speed, easy access, and short sales cycles because decision-makers are often presidents or executives, so field needs connect directly to management decisions.
Inbound tactics such as exhibitions and advertising work well in SMB, making it relatively easy to generate leads; competitor density is limited, so first-movers can more readily establish advantage.
Products that directly sell business-efficiency outcomes (reduced hassle, cost savings) fit SMB well because those effects are felt immediately and sales conversations close more easily.

Listed companies Rakus and SMS grew ARR by concentrating on SMB for years: Rakus captured universal accounting/billing needs via outbound calls and exhibitions to reach tens of thousands of customers; SMS focused on medical/nursing and enclosed many small operators.
These cases demonstrate that SMB concentration can still produce a sufficiently large company.

Core limitations of SMB focus are low average contract value and high churn: SMBs adopt quickly but also cancel quickly, are sensitive to environmental change, and often do not buy with multi-year retention in mind, so net ARR growth slows even when new bookings rise.
Sales and marketing investment-recovery efficiency therefore tends to deteriorate over time.

SMBs are highly price-sensitive; buying criteria center on cost reduction and efficiency, so willingness-to-pay (WTP) rarely rises for extra features or premium value, leaving little room for price increases or plan expansion; ARR growth therefore becomes flow-dependent (continuous new acquisition).

Customer-support load is high because many SMBs have low IT literacy, making onboarding labor-intensive; extra CS headcount is needed for retention, yet low ACV makes the investment hard to recoup, creating the dilemma of rising support cost against thin revenue and poor CS ROI.

Capital-market fit depends on time horizon: long-term compounding (as with Rakus-style multi-decade accumulation) can earn investor credit for stability, but choosing SMB concentration is a management judgment about the company’s intended growth time axis and whether it can scale efficiently on that axis.

B2B growth dilemma after PMF: whether to keep concentrating on SMB or challenge Enterprise early is a major strategic decision for executives, based on market size, company stamina/capacity, and capital-market expectations.
SMB offers short-term ease of stacking numbers and a sense of security, making it an attractive entry point for Japanese startups and enabling solid, incremental accumulation of revenue.

Continuing in SMB for further growth still requires long-term resolve and physical/organizational stamina; walls appear in the form of customer IT literacy and limited market CAP (total addressable market).
Enterprise pursuit has high hurdles: long sales/introduction cycles and large required investments in security, audits, and process readiness.
SMB structural constraints include low unit prices, high churn, and strong price sensitivity; many companies therefore plateau at roughly 1–2 billion yen in sales.

The fork that determines whether a company can cross the chasm is whether leadership has the resolve to fully commit to and ‘see through’ the SMB market, or the courage to decide to attack the next (Enterprise) market.
Many startups challenge entering the enterprise market as a path toward crossing the chasm (キャズム越え).
For companies that have already grown in the SMB market, the enterprise market is the next main stronghold (本丸).
Entering the enterprise market cannot be done by merely extending existing sales approaches and products; those are insufficient.
The requirements needed for enterprise entry are wide-ranging; whether a company can prepare them one by one determines whether it can break through this phase.
The greatest characteristics of the enterprise market are high unit prices (単価の高さ) and the complexity of the introduction/implementation process (導入プロセスの複雑さ).
Heading concept: conditions required to advance into the enterprise market.
Enterprise B2B contracts can reach tens of millions to hundreds of millions of yen in ARR from a single deal, but sales cycles typically last six months to one year and sometimes several years.

Enterprise buying involves many stakeholders beyond the target department, including information systems, security, legal, and procurement; decisions often require passing internal proposals and obtaining board/executive approval.

Startups entering the enterprise market must first satisfy non-functional requirements (e.g., audit, security). Without them, deals fail at the final stage even if sales has built relationships—common outcome: features are valued but introduction is postponed for unmet audit requirements.

For large enterprises, investments of hundreds of thousands to a few million yen may be mere budget spend or “okay to try” amounts. Winning a several-million-yen PoC can look like an opening to the enterprise market, but full production adoption is much harder.

Enterprises emphasize customization and integration: how the product connects to existing core systems and workflows, and how the vendor will support business-process change. The premise is embedding into the company’s overall operating system, not selling standalone SaaS convenience.
Product must provide APIs, SSO, and similar enterprise capabilities; sales must present scenarios of how post-implementation processes will improve.

SMB customers can change their operations to fit the product; Japanese enterprises generally will not. Success depends on fitting into existing work first, then raising convenience and organizational productivity. Overlooking this difference in dynamics is a critical mistake.
Organization must be redesigned for enterprise: SMB sales culture optimizes for speed and volume, while enterprise requires persistence—multiple people chasing one deal over a long period.

Enterprise delivery needs an integrated operating model of sales, implementation consultants, customer success, and product development, plus CxO-level executives who can engage peer-to-peer with large-company leadership, because executive-to-executive trust often drives the decision.
Trying to close enterprise deals only at the working-level “owner/担当者” layer typically fails to raise deal size.
In Japanese B2B enterprise sales, deals fail when treated as person-to-person relationships rather than as a formal “company vs. company” (会社対会社) structure and protocol.

Japan is strict about formality and rank in large transactions: enterprise buyers typically send department-head (部長) level or above, so startups should send executives (役員) or above as expected etiquette (礼儀) and protocol (作法).
Enterprise SaaS adoption often underweights implementation support and operational support compared with product features.
SMB SaaS value is often “customers can self-serve and master the product quickly”; enterprise is the opposite—failed rollout leads directly to churn.

Enterprise therefore requires a standardized, high-quality onboarding process plus professional services with intensive implementation support; buyers will pay for this because changing work for large headcount makes “not failing” the top priority.
Companies such as SmartHR and Sansan strengthened dedicated large-enterprise implementation organizations for this reason.
Professional services are often treated as a cost center, but they are a growth driver that can decide whether enterprise expansion succeeds.
PS should not be free support: it must have enough expertise and repeatability that customers pay a fair price, which also raises overall business credibility.

Successful enterprise movers prepared early: SmartHR built security and non-functional requirements, gradually formed an enterprise specialist team, and used external enterprise-sales experts for training, later exceeding ARR of 10 billion yen.

Failing companies lean on PoC deals and enter enterprise unprepared; without implementation capacity, products do not stick, logo/symbol customers are not won, PoCs grow while ARR does not, SMB resources are split, and overall growth stalls.

Enterprise expansion is an unavoidable challenge for companies in the roughly 1–2 billion yen revenue phase; required conditions include non-functional requirements, company-to-company relationship systems, and advanced implementation/professional services.
