Only companies that clear these hurdles can approach 10 billion yen scale; they should still use product and sales capability honed in SMB as weapons while building enterprise-specific capability.

In B2B growth from product-market fit (PMF) toward 10 billion yen in sales, overcoming a key scaling wall depends on whether leadership has the resolve to nearly restructure the company and form a dedicated organizational system for a specific customer segment (e.g., enterprise-oriented).
That commitment to a dedicated structure, rather than incremental tweaks, is the decisive factor that determines whether the wall can be broken through.

After a startup decides to enter the enterprise market, the next challenge is how to actually sell: SMB sales emphasize speed and volume, with direct conversations with executives or department heads to close short-term contracts, whereas enterprise is a completely different world.

Enterprise deals can reach tens of millions of yen in ARR per contract, but the evaluation process is complex, stakeholders are numerous and diverse, and sales cycles typically last six months to one year (sometimes several years); SMB methods will not work.
Enterprise sales has its own unique 'form' (型) and practical operational points; whether a company understands and prepares for them determines success or failure.

The biggest characteristic of enterprise deals is the large number of people involved in decision-making: not only the target department's manager, but also information systems, security, legal, purchasing, and audit departments participate in the review process.
In enterprise sales, one person saying 'good' is not enough to reach a contract, while a single 'NO' from any stakeholder can immediately stop the deal.

In enterprise B2B sales, salespeople must draw a stakeholder map from the start of a deal, identifying every person involved in the decision and delivering tailored messages based on each person's purchasing decision factors; without this, deals do not progress.
Enterprise purchasing typically involves an average of 5.4 people who must all be convinced, unlike SMB sales where stakeholder mapping skill is almost never required.

A primary reason startups stumble when moving from SMB to enterprise is insufficient ability to involve multiple stakeholders: even a strong relationship with a field user can still fail when legal rejects, procurement slashes price, or audit ultimately kills the deal.

Enterprise procurement frequently requires RFP (Request for Proposal) responses: procurement issues specs to multiple vendors, compares conditions, and selects a winner, forcing startups into heavy document creation, security and legal questionnaires, and detailed pricing that can consume so much resource that other company activity stops.

Procurement departments are measured on cost reduction, so they push prices below what a startup considers break-even; the required response is not simply lowering price but presenting a logical justification using ROI calculations, operational-efficiency gains, competitor comparisons, and standard SaaS market price bands compiled into materials that can convince procurement.

Enterprise deals commonly demand a PoC because the customer wants to try a small-scale implementation before committing; most PoCs are free or low-priced, creating high cost for the vendor, no immediate revenue, and frequent failure to convert into a paid contract ("PoC hell").

Healthy PoC execution requires three pre-agreed conditions: (1) a clear purpose stating exactly what will be verified and the pass/fail criteria, otherwise the PoC extends indefinitely; (2) a limited set of participating stakeholders plus a mechanism to share results; (3) contractual language that defines the conditions under which the PoC converts into a full paid contract.
If those PoC arrangements are omitted, the PoC simply consumes sales resources without producing revenue.

Enterprise sales cannot be executed by salespeople alone; presales (technical sales) or a dedicated technical-support team must run in parallel to map the customer's business flow, prove technical feasibility, and design post-implementation system integration, customizing proposals and demos to the customer's actual operations.

SMB buyers often accept standard product features, whereas enterprise buyers constantly question consistency with existing systems and compliance with security standards; without presales capability, sales cannot answer those questions and loses trust.

In B2B enterprise sales, pre-sales plays a central role in PoC (Proof of Concept) and implementation phases. Technical conversations with a customer's IT department cannot be handled by sales alone; pre-sales must take the front.
When a startup challenges enterprise customers, the first hire that is often needed is a strong pre-sales talent, because technical credibility with IT stakeholders is a prerequisite.
Top sales talent who can stand at the sales front is difficult both to hire and to develop. Therefore their productivity must be maximized rather than diluted with routine work.

The recommended operating model is ABC Sales: A = Actor (top sales talent who raises the stage of the deal); B = Bridge (person whose main job is relationship-building with the customer, overseeing the entire sales process, and assigning the right people at the right time); C = Customer.
Actor-level talent is scarce. Many companies still put top salespeople on the front line while also making them handle detailed follow-ups; this wastes high-value time.

Actors should concentrate only on work that only an Actor can do. Relationship-building and day-to-day customer request handling should be owned by Bridge, who stands in front of the customer and coordinates internal members.
Separating Actor and Bridge roles expands the number of enterprise deals the organization can handle and raises the quality of the sales process.
Bridge talent who repeatedly observe Actors in action will, over time, grow into Actors themselves. This is how enterprise sales headcount is scaled (referenced as figures 4-1 to 4-2).
The ABC Sales Model ① (ABCセールスモデル①) is a B2B enterprise sales framework that distinguishes the Actor (社長やトップセールス) from the Customer (商談担当者).
Actor role: the president or top salesperson who can change the atmosphere of the meeting (場の空気を変えられる人), including in enterprise (エンプラ) sales.
Customer role: the person in charge of the business negotiation (商談担当者) who functions as a key person (キーパーソン) whose main concern is proposal content that can be internally approved/passed (通せる提案内容).
Core process elements of the model include toss-up (トスアップ), value assignment/value-adding (価値づけ), and trust-building through pre-hearing and follow-up (事前ヒアリング／フォローによる信頼構築).
The model emphasizes matching a high-influence Actor with a Customer who cares about internally passable proposals, using pre-work and follow-up to build trust before and around the meeting.

The IABC Sales Model ② structures B2B deal progression across four sequential stages: 商談準備 (deal/meeting preparation), 初回商談 (initial meeting), 上長面談 (meeting with the prospect’s superior/manager), and クロージング (closing).

Actor is a designated high-level role that intervenes only at specific marked steps rather than owning the entire process; typical Actor actions include hypothesis review, proposal review, management-perspective feedback (経営目線のFB), speaking for only about 3 minutes, and supplying wording that the rest of the team then cites or reuses (Actorの言葉として援用).

Bridge is the primary execution role that owns the bulk of value communication (基本の価値づけ), trust-building with the superior, scenario creation (商談シナリオを100%作成), follow-up, progress checks, and most of the conversation; Actor’s contribution is limited to the final push (最後の一押しだけ).

Key supporting activities mapped onto the stages include: hypothesis formulation and sharing with the mobilizer, proposal-content creation and sharing, Actor-led reviews, follow-up calls and emails, status/progress confirmation around the superior’s proposal and contract, and setting the 上長面談.

The model emphasizes pre-work (full scenario scripting, hypothesis development, value-proposition packaging) so that live meetings stay tightly orchestrated and Actor time remains extremely short and high-leverage.

Another core principle of enterprise sales is executive-to-executive relationships (経営幹部同士のリレーション). Large companies seek 'corporate reliability' (会社としての信頼性) from trading partners; even an excellent sales rep is not enough—the perceived trustworthiness of the vendor's management team significantly influences the buyer's decision.

Executives should sit in on deals and speak directly with the customer's officers and department-head class. When tops share vision and confirm a long-term partnership, contracts can move forward rapidly.

'Trust acquisition at the management level' (経営レベルでの信頼獲得) is especially important in the Japanese market. Because 稟議 (internal approval) and decision-making take time, having management or department heads conclude 'this startup can be trusted' (このスタートアップなら任せられる) helps drive internal consensus.

Successful enterprise-sales companies share four traits: (1) they prepare non-functional requirements (非機能要件) so customers can evaluate with peace of mind; (2) they have strong salespeople who can sell into enterprises with many stakeholders and customized proposals; (3) they design PoCs so verification reliably converts to a paid contract; (4) executives personally commit to customer relationships and underwrite company-level credibility.

Failed companies treat enterprise as an extension of SMB: sales only builds relationships with field staff, technical and non-functional requirements are neglected, and unlimited PoCs are accepted. Pipeline grows but contracts do not close, resources are consumed, and the company falls into typical 'PoC hell' (PoC地獄), stalling enterprise-market entry.

Enterprise sales is a different world from SMB sales. Many stakeholders, long cycles, strict non-functional requirements, PoC design, pre-sales and implementation consulting, CS operational capability, and executive-to-executive trust all intertwine; missing even one means the deal will not close.

For startups, conquering this world is a high hurdle but a condition for reaching ¥10 billion in sales (売上100億). Do not simply carry SMB momentum into enterprise; adapt to enterprise-specific structure. The effort must be company-wide—product, CS, and management—not sales alone.
Enterprise sales (エンタープライズセールス) is not merely a sales method or technique, but a battle that tests and questions the comprehensive capabilities (総合力) of the entire company.

In enterprise B2B deals, the moment implementation is decided is not the goal; the real contest begins afterward because large companies roll out to hundreds or thousands of users and the introduction process is complex.

If usage does not become sufficiently established, the following year's contract renewal is likely to result in shrinkage or cancellation; therefore 'being usable' is insufficient and the offering must be designed so that customers continue using it and keep expanding it.

Enterprise Customer Success (CS) must thoroughly design onboarding and education systems: standardized manuals, video training materials, and training programs for the customer's internal trainers; without these, usage will not take hold inside the customer organization.

Enterprise CS is not mere support; it requires a role close to project management—formulating an implementation schedule, managing progress with stakeholders, and visualizing utilization rates—because large enterprises will not confidently continue the contract without such operational capability.
Transforming Customer Success is the way to escape dependence on new Proof-of-Concept (PoC) deals.

Redefine customer success not by feature utilization rate but by improvement in business KPIs that decision-makers (e.g., department heads) can use for quarterly-review accountability, such as labor-saving volume, error-rate reduction, shortened case lead time, and employee NPS improvement.
Break product usage down into time-series milestones so it is visible whether the improvement process is on schedule or delayed.
Enterprise customer success is per-company project management, not an extension of support.
Implementation WBS should explicitly list tasks, owners, and approval gates, and fix roles among IT, field managers, and field promoters.
Change-management plan should include announcement templates, internal FAQ, and role-specific training (managers, field staff, helpdesk) distributed in advance.
Agree activation goals such as a 90-day plan with milestones, and prepare a correction plan for missed targets.
Design pilots for staged rollout: agree success criteria and production go-live dates so PoC does not become a dead end.
The PM draws a Gantt chart and drives execution as a trinity with technical support and professional services; Who/What/How must never be left ambiguous.
Thick high-touch support is unprofitable, so these activities must be positioned as Professional Services, converting cost into revenue.

Enterprise adoption quality is determined by professional-services quality; monetize menus such as requirements definition, migration, integration, business-process design, and training, priced on outcomes and risk reduction.
Once professional services become self-running, CS can focus on operational improvement and account expansion, which raises NRR.

Enterprise CS succeeds by projectizing onboarding, measuring value with business KPIs, correcting in a data-driven way, reducing risk via professional services, and maximizing LTV through staged expansion.
Unlike SMB’s “speed × volume” model, enterprise NRR of 100%+ becomes the norm only through intentional “design × operations × agreement” that produces results by design.

In B2B growth after product-market fit (PMF), once companies overcome the key trials on the path to 10 billion yen in sales, revenue acquired from enterprise customers shifts away from dependence on new Proof of Concepts (PoCs).
That enterprise revenue then grows through reliable compound interest (複利) rather than one-off or constantly restarted PoC-driven deals.
Quote/paraphrase of the core claim: when those trials are overcome, sales obtained from enterprise companies break free of new-PoC dependence and expand with certain compounding growth.

Startups entering the enterprise-market phase typically already run partner sales; SMB-oriented agency contracts are commonly in place by the time revenue has grown from several hundred million yen to around 1 billion yen.
At the 1–2 billion yen revenue stage, enterprise-market challenges cannot be solved by simply extending the prior partner-sales model that worked for SMB expansion.

The partner model that supported SMB-centric growth must be redesigned specifically for enterprise; whether a company pauses and reconstructs this mechanism at this point determines subsequent growth.
Traditional partner sales centered on grasping industry structure, acquiring leads broadly, and obtaining deal introductions.
In SMB markets, partner methods such as following up exhibition/event leads via agencies or having regional sales partners carry products work sufficiently.
In the enterprise market those same methods are insufficient: mere introductions rarely reach decision-makers, so deals frequently stall or are lost before implementation.
Enterprise partner sales therefore require a posture of jointly attacking accounts rather than simple referrals.
Enterprise deals are long-term, multi-department campaigns that involve sales, IT systems, security, legal, and purchasing; opposition from any single stakeholder can stop the deal.

Partner sales must be redefined: move from a pure reseller/agency model to partners capable of joint proposals and joint project execution, and of granting access to their proprietary information assets.

Concrete tactics include joint proposals that assume integration with an SIer’s existing custom core systems, and strategic account-based selling that leverages a major agency’s installed customer base.
This shift is from quantity-oriented SMB selling to quality-oriented enterprise selling.

Partner selection criteria also change. SMB expansion values channel breadth, number of salespeople (touch-points), and product fit. Enterprise expansion values expertise and reliability above those metrics.
Customers judge partners on how well they understand the buyer’s industry and how far they can satisfy non-functional and security requirements.
Partners that can cover the domains a startup cannot reach directly become indispensable for enterprise conquest.
Selection therefore switches from “how much can they sell?” to “how far can they move the customer forward together?”

The relationship itself must evolve from deal-by-deal transactions to strategic collaboration: joint marketing, joint seminars, joint proposals, and sitting at the same table with the customer while dividing implementation roles.
To make that possible, partners need thorough education, information sharing, certification programs, training, and a regular-update mechanism so they can propose with confidence.
Large partners handle many products, so for a startup’s product to be sold preferentially they must themselves believe that “this product can win” and that “customers value it.”
A practical way to earn that belief is to co-create symbolic customers (シンボル顧客) with the partner and let the partner use those success stories as a sales weapon.
Enterprise-oriented partner sales should therefore be designed around “creating symbolic case studies” (シンボル事例づくり) rather than generic channel enablement.
A second major challenge is the speed gap: startups treat speed as a weapon, while SIers and large distributors decide inside complex organizations and often cannot move at startup pace.
To close the speed gap, the startup must explicitly decide which work the partner owns and which work the company itself leads, cutting unnecessary coordination cost.
Example of role split: the partner owns core-system connection requirements; the company itself leads deal flow and proposal materials.
Avoid the binary of “leave everything to the partner” vs. “do everything in-house”; role-cutting is the required design lens.
Rebuilding enterprise partner sales also requires internal capability: dedicated alliance managers, per-partner strategy and goals, deal-progress management, and shared results.
The partner team must work cross-functionally with sales and CS and rapidly feed customer feedback back into the product.
Because customers are won through partners, learnings from those deals must be returned in-house or competitiveness will not be sharpened.
Firms that succeed at this reconstruction open markets that direct sales alone could not reach.
Successful companies do not treat partners merely as a “sales channel” but position them as a “community for market conquest” (市場攻略の共同体).

In the ¥1–2 billion sales phase of Japanese B2B startups, partner sales must be reconstructed rather than continuing the SMB-phase model; systems and organization must be rebuilt to match enterprise-specific deal structures.

Partner-sales reconstruction in this phase requires: clarifying deal sources, thorough role division, co-creating with symbol (flagship) customers, building education programs, and operational capability that closes speed-gap differences with partners.

Companies that reconstruct partner sales can pioneer markets together with partners and build a foothold toward ¥10 billion in sales; whether partner sales can be rebuilt is a decisive factor for the next stage of growth.
The ¥1–2 billion (10–20 oku yen) range is one of the toughest walls for Japanese B2B startups: growth-curve slope often flattens and companies fear they are hitting a ceiling.
The wall is produced by interacting factors: insufficient market thickness, limits of SMB dependence, and the high requirements of enterprise expansion—momentum alone cannot break through.
Few companies cross this wall; those that do can then draw a realistic path toward ARR of ¥10 billion scale.
The chasm is not the end of growth but a test of whether the company can install the next growth engine.

Successful firms faced reality and refused to stay on a linear extension of existing tactics; they chose calmly between concentrating on SMB or attacking enterprise based on market size and their own strengths, and did not postpone necessary preparations.
Investment in non-functional requirements and professional services looks like a short-term burden but becomes the long-term foundation for enterprise conquest.
Creating symbol (flagship) customers is not mere track-record building; it is the strongest weapon for winning the next customers.
Stagnant companies tell themselves they can still ‘dig more’ in SMB and then plateau for years; PoC volume rises without converting to full contracts, depleting sales resources.

Partner sales introduced only in form, without enterprise-appropriate reconstruction, fails to move deals; avoiding required investment and postponing decisions leaves many firms stalled in the low-teens of billions of yen in sales.

In the BtoB growth phase of roughly 1–2 billion yen in sales (売上10億〜20億円), companies cannot avoid structural challenges such as hitting the limits of SMB dependency, accumulating PoC deals that fail to convert into full contracts (wasting resources), or postponing the build-out of implementation-support organizations and partner programs.

Two decisive questions must be answered at this stage: (1) Where is the company’s core market (本丸市場)—deepening SMB or moving into enterprise? (2) Has the company actually operationalized the capabilities required to win in that market (non-functional requirements / 非機能要件, implementation support / 導入支援, organizational structure, and rebuilt partner-sales motion) rather than leaving them “in preparation”?

The chasm (キャズム) is produced by external market structure, yet whether a company can cross it is determined by internal decision-making: the willingness to calmly identify the true market, commit the necessary investment, and rebuild the organization.

Only companies that make these commitments and operationalize the required capabilities can advance to the next growth stage; postponing preparation in front of the 2-billion-yen wall typically prevents crossing the chasm.
Key diagnostic for leadership: Has the firm chosen its core market, installed the next growth engine, and stopped treating implementation support and partner systems as future work?
Safie Inc. (セーフィー株式会社) was founded on October 23, 2014. It develops, operates, and provides related services for the cloud recording-type video platform 'Safie'.
The company implements AI on video data to contribute to solving social issues across industries, including on-site DX (現場DX) and labor shortages.
CEO Ryuhei Sadojima (佐渡島隆平) joined Sony Network Communications in 2002, became CMO of Sony-funded Motion Portrait Inc. in 2010, and founded Safie in 2014.
Safie achieved the No.1 share in cloud recording services in 2017. The CEO ranked 1st in the Forbes JAPAN Japan Entrepreneurs Ranking 2021.
Company vision: 'Creating the future from video' (映像から未来をつくる). It promotes on-site DX across all industries through utilization of video data.

In anticipation of an advancing population-decline '8-gake society' (8がけ社会), Safie promotes operational efficiency and more advanced decision-making via video data, aiming to build next-generation social infrastructure.
The book frames B2B startup growth from PMF to 10 billion yen in sales around five common 'walls' (trials) that companies must overcome, with corresponding responses at each step.

Safie's publicly disclosed growth graph appears smoothly upward from around 2020, but the CEO states the actual seeds of growth were planted in 2015–2019 (ARR of 1.195 billion yen as of end-December 2019).

Building hardware, converting it to a recurring/subscription (リカーリング) business model, and creating a market from zero involved extreme hardship; the period until ARR reached 100 million yen was described as very painful.
It took 3.5 years to reach 100 million yen ARR; the CEO felt that almost all of the book's five walls were condensed into this early struggle.
Safie originally launched as a B2C company via crowdfunding.

Early B2C sales looked successful but were a 'nuka-yorokobi' (false joy / premature celebration). Approximately 3,000 manufactured cameras suffered a fatal hardware-venture failure: they were hard to connect to Wi-Fi.
The pivot to B2B (especially the construction market) was not a strategic choice but a necessity: 'we had no choice but to go B2B' because they had to sell off 3,000 units of inventory.

While desperately trying to move inventory, they discovered that major general contractors (ゼネコン) and construction-materials companies were already customizing the consumer cameras for construction-site use, which became the trigger for the B2B direction.
Cloud cameras for construction sites needed to transmit over 5 GB of data per day, but contemporaneous pocket Wi-Fi used mobile lines with a 2 GB cap, creating a major communications barrier.

Japan's first uplink-only SIM was developed by exploiting surplus uplink bandwidth inside an MVNO (mobile virtual network operator) arrangement, based on the traffic asymmetry that far more users consume video (downlink, e.g. YouTube) than upload it.
The uplink-only SIM enabled a simple 'just plug the power in' deployment model and triggered a full pivot into the construction industry.

The 'Othello Four Corners Strategy' treats B2B scale-up as a game of capturing the four corner positions of a market rather than selling hardware by hand; the insight came from an ORIX executive who said 'do not sell cameras yourself' and 'Othello is won from the four corners.'

The four corner players identified were: sensor/device manufacturers, communications infrastructure, security companies, and power companies plus developers (equipment and urban fabric); distribution and hardware-finance (rental) were added as additional critical pieces.
A joint rental business with ORIX supplied the financial leverage needed to scatter hardware at scale.
Investors were required to give genuine operational commitment, not merely capital: investment contracts stipulated seconded personnel and jointly executed sales plans.

BtoB growth from PMF toward large-scale sales requires partnership schemes that include concrete offers such as providing hardware and collaborating, in order to build allies and a scaling organization.
Integrating distribution strategy with capital policy around a key partner (example: ORIX as key person) can finally put a scaling structure in place.
A partnership strategy can help startups simultaneously cross the chasm (the wall of expanding to enterprise customers and regional markets).

Crossing that wall depends on thorough product polishing: simplify until even older, IT-unfamiliar frontline workers can use the product just by turning on the power, and never force time-consuming setup (UX that enables easy introduction in both regional and enterprise settings).
The product work is a direct response to the shared need that 'nobody wants to spend effort there' (現場DX / field DX).
After a product-out, concentrate on knocking down the 'center pin': the single most influential person in that industry.
In Who / What / How, specify Who down to the level of literally one person in the industry (example: XX-san of ○○ Construction in construction) and meet that person's requests at all costs.

CEO, CTO, and the whole team go to the customer's site, feel the customer's 'fu' (pain/dissatisfaction) firsthand, and solve it; once the industry center pin recognizes the company, expansion across that industry accelerates.

A B2B company spun out from Sony deliberately rejected becoming a single-industry vertical (e.g., construction only) from day one, because the founder wanted to build a globally competitive platform; even ¥10 billion in revenue was treated as a waypoint, not the destination.
The long-term vision was framed as 'from home to the city, tackle everything' in order to capture data across the entire physical environment rather than remaining inside one vertical.

In 2012, at the appearance of deep learning, the founder identified the core insight that 'data itself is life,' while simultaneously forecasting that the practical wave would take roughly a decade to arrive.

Field AI (on-site AI) becomes implementable only after three conditions coincide: widespread iPhone adoption, cheap semiconductor chips, and low-power cameras that can be embedded in the field; this combination was estimated to require about 10 years.

The lag from basic-technology invention to established use-cases and cost reduction is typically 10–20 years; the historical example given is the gap between FeliCa development and the mass adoption of Suica.

Therefore the company executed a 10-year-ahead data-collection strategy covering 'everything from home to city' so that it would already possess the necessary data when the technology and cost curves finally aligned.

This timing discipline is compared to Nintendo’s 'lateral thinking of withered (mature) technology': crossing the chasm depends on waiting until the technology is sufficiently mature and the economics become viable.
Despite being a hardware-plus-software startup that must manage a full supply chain (procurement through installation), cumulative employee turnover remained extremely low until IPO.

Because the business is not pure SaaS, the company invested heavily in 'companion-building' that deliberately included customers, partner firms, and investors as stakeholders who share both the hardship and the rewards.

The organizational philosophy is an application of the Japanese 'sanpo yoshi' (three-way satisfaction) principle together with the cultural values of 'wa' (harmony) and 'jin' (benevolence): never betray companions and ensure that everyone who contributed is properly rewarded.
Stock options were granted to all employees as part of aligning the organization.
A distinctive “different organism” (異オー体) culture is implemented thoroughly, with the Culture Deck placed at the center of every strategy.
Core operating belief: culture beats strategy (文化は戦略に勝る).
Talent philosophy: everyone has talent (すべての人は才能がある).
HR system is built on two axes—Expert × Management—and is finely customized to the company’s own philosophy rather than used off-the-shelf.
The HR and organizational design is tuned according to growth phase.
After listing, the growth engine is changed by launching new businesses while rapidly advancing organizational changes.
Early-stage survival and later growth were supported by two named strategies: the Othello four-corners strategy (オセロ四隅戦略) and the center-pin strategy (センターピン戦略).

After ~7 years from founding, a B2B company can reach ARR of 30 oku yen (3 billion yen) once enterprise expansion succeeds through company-wide transformation rather than isolated sales effort; major-enterprise deals then begin closing in sequence and internal momentum toward IPO can appear.

Management must stay realistic: single-product growth has a near-term ceiling set by addressable market size; without a second growth pillar the business will eventually plateau even if current sales are strong.
Once the core business can be delegated to a COO plus sales lead, the founder/CEO’s job shifts from day-to-day operations to “drawing the next growth” (次の成長を描くこと).

A common founder move at this stage is to scan market trends, pick a “future-potential” theme, pull the most talented internal people, and launch an independent new-business team reporting directly to the CEO, framing the talent drain as “an investment in the future” despite operational push-back that “the existing business will stop running if people leave.”

The story’s framing (“chasing a rabbit and ending up looking at the sky”) signals that this talent-extraction + independent-team approach is presented as a high-risk trial that companies must navigate between PMF and 100-oku-yen scale.

A common B2B growth trap: launching a new product aimed at a market adjacent to the original customer base (similar industry, but a slightly different problem structure), then treating brand recognition and rising meeting volume as proof the product will work.

Brand awareness can increase inbound willingness to take a first meeting (“we’ll hear you out because you’re Company X”), but that does not equal product-market fit or conversion; demos can feel positive while later stages stall and deals fail to close.

A diagnostic pattern of misalignment: pipeline volume is high, first-demo reactions are favorable, yet follow-up dies and win rates stay low—something is off in problem, buyer, or value, even if the team cannot yet name it.

Diverting talent to a new product can damage the core business: slower product development, weaker support quality, openings for later competitors to attack on price, and churn among key existing customers, which then poisons team morale.

Customers won on the new product may have different attributes from the original customer set, so they do not enable cross-sell or upsell; the “second pillar” then fails both as a growth engine and as a synergy play.

Strategic purpose can silently drift: the original intent was to build a second revenue pillar, but “doing something new” becomes the goal itself, while the existing business is still unfinished and the new bet targets a slightly distant market.
Spreading the team without a sharp direction produces the two-hares problem: both the core business and the new product remain incomplete rather than one becoming a durable pillar.

Implication for PMF-to-scale: polish and defend the existing business before stretching into nearby-but-structurally-different markets; otherwise resource split, weak conversion, and lost synergy compound at once.

The 'multi-product swamp' (マルチプロダクトの沼) is a growth-phase trap in which companies, after an existing product's growth slows, attempt to launch a second business pillar; organizational energy disperses and both the existing business and the new business stagnate.

Most B2B SaaS companies encounter this situation once revenue reaches the 2–4 billion yen range: the first product has captured a certain market share, sales/CS/marketing processes are established, and the organization has become stable.
At that stage executives typically feel urgency to 'create a second pillar' (第2の柱をつくらなければ); investors also push for new-business exploration and an internal mood for the next challenge emerges.
The impulse is a natural and unavoidable challenge for growing companies, yet many sink into the swamp because what looks like positive investment actually fragments focus.
The swamp is therefore a distinctive risk of the growth phase rather than a failure of ambition itself.

The biggest trap in the post-PMF growth phase (toward ~¥10B sales) is resource dispersion: launching new businesses requires reallocating three finite resources—people, capital, and time—from existing operations.

When leadership gets excited about a 'new challenge,' top talent is pulled from the core business, internal balance collapses, the new venture still generates no revenue, existing output drops, and both businesses stall.

Dispersion is not only human resources: meeting agendas dualize, development priorities become ambiguous, and the executive team's attention splits in two, so the company as a whole loses the power of concentration.
The 'multiproduct swamp' is the state in which resources are scattered and organizational focus has collapsed.

Founding-era success patterns actively encourage later dispersion. Early on, the winning formula was to move scarce resources at all costs: read the market by intuition and speed, ship first and catch up later, work around the clock, and rely on team grit ('the smelly way of winning').

Once ARR exceeds ~¥3B, speed-only execution becomes a risk. 'Ship first, think later' that was tolerated in the founding stage can now destroy trust; product quality, security, legal, and support all require organizational consistency that 'just try it' no longer satisfies.

Many CEOs unconsciously try to replay the founding playbook (intuitive market selection + speed breakthrough), which breaks existing operations and exhausts teams. The very success pattern that worked at founding becomes a liability in the next growth phase.

A second trap is the illusion created by brand power. Around ¥3B in revenue the company name and founder become known, booths attract attention, media coverage appears, and prospects say 'we'll take a meeting because it's Company X.' Deal volume and conversation quality rise, producing a false sense of success.

Early-stage customer reactions were earned through passion and repeated hypothesis testing; later they arrive 'for free' via brand. Teams therefore feel 'traction' that is often only 'being listened to,' not 'actually resonating' or converting.

The 'second phantom PMF' (第2の幻のPMF) occurs in growing companies when brand tailwind makes early reactions to a new venture look like success, causing management to pull people and time from the core business and over-invest in the new one.
Unlike the founding stage, the illusion of PMF is stronger after initial success because of existing brand, so the problem is often noticed only after it has become a major issue.

Launching a new business after one success is substantially harder than founding: markets are mature, customers have many alternatives, almost no 'white-space' markets remain, and growing firms lack the multi-year trial-and-error slack of the startup phase.
Investors and employees demand 'next growth,' compressing validation into 1–2 years; only the speed of resource injection increases, not the quality of learning.
Pouring resources does not produce results; misapplied force can stall both the existing and the new business at once.
Companies fall into a 'chasing two hares' (二兎を追う) structure: the core business faces rising pressure just to maintain revenue while the new business is asked for numbers without having achieved PMF.
Development and sales cannot decide priorities; management meetings repeatedly debate 'which to grow' and 'where to invest,' slowing decisions.
From the outside the firm appears to be expanding; in reality resources are dispersed and focus is lost. This is the true nature of the multi-product swamp (マルチプロダクトの沼).
Growth is stopped not by the market but by internal structure—specifically distortion in resource allocation.
The moment executives declare they will 'build a second pillar,' they are forced into the most difficult trade-offs of resource allocation.
In B2B growth (from PMF toward 10 billion yen in sales), resource design should shift from merely dividing resources to designing so that resources are utilized/leveraged.
Do not rely on past success patterns or brand power; instead, identify where the company should concentrate.
The essence of a multi-product strategy is not simply expanding the business, but identifying the domains where the company can demonstrate its strengths and concentrating again on those areas.
When B2B companies exceed roughly 2–3 billion yen in revenue, many executives begin to feel they may stall if they continue as-is; a single product has a real ceiling.
Single-product growth is constrained by market-size limits, little remaining room to raise prices, and depletion of the original target segment—all of which flatten the growth curve.

The typical next language from founders who feel this ceiling is “build a second pillar” or “expand into an adjacent domain.” That is not optional ambition; it is a requirement for sustainable growth.
Almost without exception, companies that have reached a certain scale must become multi-product in order to move to the next stage of growth.
The section frames multi-productization as the way to simultaneously address two constraints: number of customers and willingness to pay (WTP).
Key framing: customer count and WTP make multi-productization inevitable once a company has scaled past PMF toward the 10-billion-yen revenue range.

Japan's B2B market is characterized by slow service penetration: even excellent products do not dramatically accelerate intra-company adoption because decisions require multi-department approvals and implementation involves internal coordination; winning a single customer often takes 6 months to 1 year.

Early-stage high growth typically comes from rapidly capturing the early-adopter layer; around ¥2 billion in revenue that layer saturates, leaving slower, more conservative enterprises, which lengthens the growth cycle.

Companies that can treat time as an ally (e.g., Obic, Yayoi) can still exceed ¥10 billion in revenue with a single product by steadily expanding adoption over many years; this path is viable when time-axis pressure is low.

Startups facing investor expectations and rapid organizational-growth demands cannot use the same long-horizon strategy; the mismatch between 'it will grow if given time' and 'we cannot afford time' is the first structural reason multi-product expansion becomes inevitable.

Vertical SaaS faces an even tighter constraint: the addressable number of companies is far smaller than in horizontal SaaS, so the customer-count (logo) growth driver hits a ceiling sooner and growth must shift toward raising ARPA via multi-product.

A second structural wall of a single product is the customer's willingness-to-pay (WTP) ceiling for one problem: adding features that still solve the same problem does not materially raise WTP, and simply raising price encounters psychological and economic resistance.
Therefore, increasing unit economics is more effective by expanding the number of problems solved than by raising the price of a single-problem product.

SmartHR illustrates the shift: it began with labor-procedure efficiency, then expanded into adjacent problems (talent management, HR evaluation, organizational-data utilization) for the same customer base, thereby lifting WTP and ARPA.

Sticking to a single product causes an early encounter with the WTP ceiling—a universal phenomenon independent of industry or customer size—so companies must eventually move the growth axis from 'raise price' to 'increase the number of problems solved.'

The WTP limit is the structural turning point that makes multi-product strategy necessary; exceptions exist only for firms that can use time as an ally or that have already established an extremely high customer-unit-price structure.

An exceptional B2B growth pattern (illustrated by Sansan) is expanding value from a narrow offering such as business-card management to a broader one such as a customer-contact database, thereby redefining the existing market and enabling long-term growth. This market-redefinition path is rare, not the default.
To sustain growth speed after PMF, a company must strengthen either customer count or unit price (ARPU). Customer expansion is slow; unit-price upside is capped by WTP (willingness to pay).
The only way to overcome both constraints at once—slow customer-base growth and a WTP ceiling on price—is multi-productization (マルチプロダクト化).

Multi-productization is not an optional ‘challenge’ or mere diversification strategy; it is a structural necessity. It is the evolutionary form companies are forced into if they want continued growth.

Staying a single-product company and still growing is theoretically possible, but it requires time that startups typically do not have. Hence firms naturally move toward a multi-product model to break the twin limits of customer numbers and WTP.
The following section (promised in the text) examines how to design a multi-product strategy so it succeeds, and under what conditions it fails, using real case studies.

When advancing multi-productization, the first branching point is deciding which domain to expand the next product into; a wrong first move causes organization design, sales design, and business structure to all go off track afterward.
Successful companies draw an expansion path starting from their own strengths; failing companies jump into new areas starting from the external environment or trends.
Even under the same 'multi-product' label, a difference in starting point (internal strengths vs. external trends) produces a fatal gap years later.
Successful multi-product companies follow two main patterns: (1) solving adjacent problems for the same customers, and (2) horizontally expanding the same business model into other domains.
The same-customer / adjacent-problem pattern raises ARPA (Average Revenue Per Account) by digging deeper into existing customers.
The same-business-model / horizontal-expansion pattern reuses existing mechanisms to acquire new markets.
Successful multi-product B2B companies share a common starting point: how to leverage their existing strengths rather than chasing unrelated opportunities.

SmartHR grew from a single product (labor-procedure efficiency) into adjacent problems of the same customers: talent management, personnel evaluation, and organizational data analysis, without leaving the core HR/labor market.

The royal road of multi-product strategy is to keep targeting the same industry and department as existing customers while expanding the problems you solve horizontally; trust with current customers then enables cross-sell and creates synergy across product, sales, and support.

Salesforce followed the same pattern: CRM as the foundation, then stacked sales, marketing, customer-support, and analytics modules while consistently holding the axis of strengthening customer relationships.

Successful multi-productization begins with deepening the existing market (unsolved problems of current customers), not exploring entirely new markets; this dramatically raises the probability of success.

A second successful pattern is to take the same business model into different markets. Raksul (Lacul) reused the mechanisms built in print e-commerce—platform operation, demand-supply matching, and production optimization—across advertising, logistics, and human resources.

Raksul’s strength is that even when the industry domain changes, the core value proposition (“industry transformation through a platform”) stays consistent, so existing operations, technology, and data can be reused at scale.

Across both patterns, successful firms capture new markets as an extension of their own strengths; multi-productization is therefore the repositioning and expansion of strengths, not merely adding more businesses.
A common trait of failed multi-product efforts is dispersing resources rather than concentrating them along a coherent strength axis.

Failing companies often conceive new businesses from the external environment rather than internal strengths: e.g. 'this product is growing overseas,' 'this domain has a large market size,' or 'there are no competitors yet.' These look attractive on the surface.

Entering a market based primarily on its size means facing a completely different customer profile. Sales channels differ, decision-makers differ, and the structure of provided value changes. Synergy with the existing business disappears and internal know-how can no longer be applied.
The common complaint that 'the market is large but it doesn't grow' is typically caused by this structural mismatch between the new market and the company's existing assets.

A typical failure pattern is launching a product that leaves the industry or job type of existing customers. Example: an HR/labor SaaS company developing a sales-support tool. Superficially both are B2B SaaS and therefore 'close,' but customer understanding (resolution) and sales rhythm are completely different. The new business therefore becomes a restart from zero and doubly consumes management resources.

Three conditions that raise the success probability of choosing a new market (derived from successful multi-product companies): (1) Overlap of existing customers and the new product's target—whether the product can be sold without creating an entirely new channel is the first judgment criterion. (2) Continuity of issues—solve the problem that sits 'next to' the issues customers currently have; target the next pain on the same business process. (3) Consistency of provided value—the offering must not diverge from the company's core competence; every product should still feel like 'this company's style.'

When all three conditions are met, the success probability of multi-product expansion rises dramatically. The more a company deviates from them, the more resources are dispersed and the balance of the existing business begins to collapse.
Ansoff's matrix is recommended as the judgment framework for organizing these market-expansion decisions.

Ansoff's Matrix is a classic yet highly versatile framework for designing multi-product expansion strategy, using market (existing vs. new) on the vertical axis and product (existing vs. new) on the horizontal axis.
Among the four Ansoff quadrants, existing market × new product has the highest probability of success.

The four Ansoff quadrants are: existing market × existing product (deepening the existing business); existing market × new product (expansion into adjacent customer problems); new market × existing product (market development); new market × new product (diversification).
The most reliable path to compounding growth is solving adjacent problems of existing customers in the existing-market × new-product zone; this is the sweet spot of multi-product strategy.

Figure 5.1 (multi-product market selection) maps related tactics such as new-product development, related products and feature additions, increasing repeat purchase rate and purchase amount of existing products, new-market development (e.g., overseas expansion or new customer segments), and diversification as a way to capture additional revenue opportunities.
Expansion (growth) models can be made concrete by applying Ansoff's matrix; two representative directions are the LTV cross-sell stacking type and the B-to-C shift type.
The LTV cross-sell stacking model adds new products that solve adjacent problems of existing customers, raising ARPA (average revenue per account) and NRR (net revenue retention).
PLAID illustrates this: with the CX platform KARTE as the core, it cross-sells data analysis, marketing support, advertising integration, and other services, lifting NRR above 109% from 2023 onward.
Designing a multi-product lineup to raise existing-customer LTV is described as the most stable and highly reproducible growth pattern.
The B-to-C shift model uses the customer base and data assets built in an existing B2B business to widen value delivery into the consumer (toC) domain.
