UniFa is a representative B2B-to-B2C expansion example: it stacked LTV with childcare-industry toB products (safety/security, development support, operational support) then expanded to a parent-facing toC service called “ICT Hub.” It first built operational-efficiency and information-sharing systems for nurseries, then used parent contact points to introduce toC products, converting existing customer assets into a new market. This is described as an evolved form of cross-sell.
Cross-sell type sits in the “existing market × product” quadrant and expands by stacking LTV on the current customer base.
B-to-C shift type is closer to “new market × existing product” and expands by spreading horizontally into adjacent customer segments while reusing existing products/assets.
Both patterns share the same core: they create the next growth axis by leveraging existing customer relationships, data, and brand assets rather than starting from zero.

The highest-risk pattern is the “isolated-island / jumping” type: completely different new market × new product. It tends to disperse organization, talent, and brand; business-to-business synergy is hard to generate; success probability is estimated below 10%. It can look attractive but is usually unrealistic.

Practical starting point: first consider models that reuse existing assets—either LTV-stacking cross-sell centered on current customers or a B-to-C shift—before attempting distant new-market/new-product bets.

The most important criterion when choosing multi-product markets is “how far can we still fight on the ground where we are already winning?” Market size matters less than the company’s own customer understanding, implementation know-how, and brand trust. Successful firms treat “can we leverage these assets?” as the primary judgment axis.

Multi-product win/loss is decided more by where you fight than by how you fight. Select markets by customer-resolution (depth of understanding) rather than by market attractiveness; that is the key to sustained growth.
After market selection, the next required step is designing the organizational structure that will actually execute multi-product expansion.
In the multi-product stage, the first challenge when executing a multi-product strategy is the cracking (崩壊) of organizational structure.
A company that grew on a single product has sales, development, and CS all facing the same direction, with fast decision-making and a single shared goal—a monolithic organization.
The moment a second and third product launch, that monolithic structure easily fractures.
Ambiguous rules around who decides, where to allocate resources, and how to measure results cause the organization—not the products—to break first.
Multi-productization is not merely adding more businesses; it is a process of redesigning the management (経営) structure.
Key quote: Multi-productization is not simply increasing businesses, but a process of redesigning the corporate/management structure.
Key quote: If decision, resource, and measurement rules stay vague, the first thing that collapses is the organization, not the product.

When companies pursue multi-productization, three typical organizational failure patterns appear if structure is not changed: dualized responsibility, ambiguous resource allocation, and culture split.

Dualized responsibility: launching a new business as a CEO-direct initiative creates two decision-making lines with existing business owners; the field becomes confused about whose instructions to prioritize and speed drops.

Ambiguous resource allocation: keeping talent, budget, and development resources in the same organization without a clear split between existing and new businesses produces a scramble; management meetings stall on which side gets engineers or priority, and execution stops.

Culture split: the new-business team develops a different culture from the existing team, creating an oppositional narrative of 'new creates the future' versus 'existing supports the company,' which erodes trust.
These failure phenomena all result from attempting multi-productization without changing structure; single-product decision-making, evaluation, and org design cannot run multiple businesses.
Organizational structure typically evolves through three stages as a company moves to multi-product.

Integrated Model (verification phase): operate the new product as part of the existing organization. Strengths are fast information sharing and flexible use of existing resources. Once signs of success appear, ownership must be clarified early, or rotating responsibility and vague resource allocation continue.
Dedicated Model (PMF exploration phase): spin the new business out as an independent team, often under the CEO, to combine speed with concentrated accountability.

For new products or initiatives, decide the 'exit design' (出口設計) from the start: whether the effort will later be integrated into an existing business or spun out as a separate business unit. Without this decision, it risks remaining a perpetual 'president's project' (社長プロジェクト).

In the scale phase, when multiple products are stably generating revenue, the ideal structure is a business-unit system with a CPO: assign a business manager (CM) to each product, overseen by a CPO (Chief Product Officer).
The CPO judges from an overall-optimization perspective which products to invest in and which functions/features to commonize. Executives must shift role from 'player' to 'portfolio manager'.

In the multi-product phase, the executive's role must change from founding-stage leadership ('solving customer problems and polishing products') to designing structure and running the company via systems. They decide which businesses get which KPIs, where to allocate investment, and where to withdraw—shifting from individual-business 'owner' to overall portfolio manager.

Once products multiply, the next critical question is sales-organization design: how to sell new products and how to deliver them to existing customers. This 'redesign of how to sell' determines multi-product success.

Multi-product companies face a choice between an integrated ('one-stop') sales model and a specialized/divided sales model. Both have successful examples; the optimum depends on the company's customer structure and business phase.

One-stop sales model (customer-centric, all products handled by one salesperson): a single salesperson works across multiple products and makes optimal proposals based on the customer's issues. Cited examples include SmartHR, HQ, and Otsuka Shokai (大塚商会).

Two main sales organization models exist for B2B companies expanding from PMF toward large-scale revenue with multiple products: (1) one-stop sales (ワンストップセールス型), where the same sales rep sells all products, and (2) product-division / product-specialized sales (プロダクト分業型), where each product has its own dedicated business unit and sales/marketing/CS.

One-stop sales unifies the customer contact point so one trusted rep can switch proposals by customer need; this makes cross-sell more natural and tends to raise LTV. SmartHR uses this model (same reps sell labor-management and talent-management services). HQ has also adopted it, with systematic product training so reps can switch proposals. It resembles Otsuka Shokai’s long-running “one-stop IT solution sales,” in which sales act as the customer’s single window and hub, proposing hardware, software, maintenance, and cloud together while specialist internal teams deliver.

Keyence also has one salesperson handle the full product line, but with a different purpose: product-driven efficiency (one person owns visit, demo, and close) rather than customer-value-centric one-stop service. Thus Keyence optimizes sales speed/efficiency; Otsuka-style one-stop is customer-hub oriented.

Benefits of one-stop sales: consistent customer relationship, easier add-on proposals and long-term account building. Costs: high load on reps; education cost and information volume grow as the product catalog grows. The model works best when products share overlapping customer segments and similar problem structures.

Product-division model (example: Rakus) gives each SaaS (e.g., Rakuraku Seisan, Rakuraku Meisai, Mail Dealer) its own dedicated sales org that owns lead generation through close and support. Per-product KPIs are clear and energy can be concentrated on one market, yielding fast ramp-up and a highly reproducible sales motion. Strengths: specialization and focus; can serve products with very different market structures or customer bases. Weaknesses: lost inter-business synergy and fragmented customer/lead data. Mitigation: company-wide CRM/SFA and explicit lead-sharing rules.
Sales model choice should be driven by customer structure and company growth phase, not by a one-size-fits-all template.
Neither of the two B2B sales models is universally correct; the right choice depends on the company's customer structure and business phase.
One-stop sales model (examples: SmartHR, HQ, ARS): appropriate when customer segments overlap and there is large cross-sell potential.
Product-division / product-specialized sales model (example: Raksul): appropriate when customer segments or introducing departments differ by product.
Typical evolution path: start with a one-stop model using existing sales to test cross-sell, then migrate to a business-unit structure when a new business targets a different customer layer.
Sales organization design is tightly coupled with organizational-structure redesign.
Adding products is not just a product decision; it requires redesigning sales mechanisms, evaluation systems, CRM, and information-sharing as part of overall management design.
Multi-productization is the moment a company must evolve from an organization that grows individual businesses into an organization that designs structure.
Leadership must evolve from player to portfolio manager; sales must evolve from selling a single product to proposing overall customer value.
Both unifying customer contact (SmartHR-style) and deepening product-specific expertise (Raksul-style) can succeed; the optimum depends on the firm's strengths and customer structure.
What matters is not increasing the number of products itself, but how organization and sales are redesigned.
The essence of multi-product strategy is not expansion of the number of businesses but evolution of the management structure.
Organization and sales redesign determine whether the second growth stage succeeds.

In B2B growth after PMF (toward ~10 billion yen revenue), multi-product plays such as cross-sell and B-to-C shift address expanding 'what' and 'to whom'; a parallel axis that further lifts growth rate is pricing—'how much to sell for.'
Adding products increases both the justification (根拠) and the room/leeway (余地) to raise prices.
Multi-product strategy is itself a design for raising ARPA (Average Revenue Per Account).
Pricing strategy is a major theme in this phase and is framed as the greatest lever to embed into company culture.
The section transitions from the overall multi-product picture to a focused treatment of pricing strategy.

A 1% change in price can change operating profit by more than 10%. McKinsey analysis of 2,400+ global companies found that among sales volume, variable costs, fixed costs, and price, a 1% improvement in price has the largest impact on operating profit.

Raising price by 1% improves operating profit by about 11–13% on average. The same 1% improvement in sales volume contributes only about 3% to profit, and variable-cost reduction about 8%. Thus how much you charge (price) has far greater management impact than how much you sell (volume).

In stock/subscription businesses such as SaaS the effect is even larger. OpenView research reports that about 30% of ARR growth comes from price revisions. Pricing optimization is therefore the most powerful, shortest-path lever for business growth.

In an inflationary environment with rising labor and development costs, leaving prices unchanged is economically irrational. Major SaaS tools (Salesforce, Slack, Zoom, Confluence, etc.) raise prices annually; not matching cost inflation is a poor management decision.

Price revision is not betrayal of customers; it is the act of converting delivered value into appropriate revenue. In Japan a lingering mindset that “price increase = bad” leads many firms to avoid raise negotiations. Globally this view is outdated: Western SaaS companies treat price updates as a routine management activity (1–2 times per year), framed as “reassessing value and updating price,” which contributes to growth-rate differences.

The main fear of price increases is higher churn. Some churn does occur, but decisions should compare the revenue gain from the increase against the revenue loss from churn. In most cases the net revenue impact of a raise greatly exceeds churn losses.

Even if the net is roughly break-even, retaining only higher-unit-price customers lowers customer-management costs and improves profit margins. Raising unit price and concentrating on a narrower customer set is not inherently negative; it can healthy the operating structure.

After a price increase, actual churn is often smaller than expected; most executive concerns about raising prices are close to unfounded assumptions. Excessive caution creates opportunity loss and slows the speed of business expansion.
Switching costs create a 'defense' (price protection) that suppresses churn and helps customers accept price revisions.
Switching cost is the psychological, time-related, and economic burden that occurs when a customer switches to another service. In SaaS these costs can be designed intentionally.

Do not raise switching costs by increasing learning/onboarding difficulty. Prefer designs where 'the more the customer uses the product, the more data accumulates,' and relationships in which support staff understand the customer's business processes so the product becomes more than a mere tool.
Lock-in and network externalities are important additional ways to raise switching costs.

Lock-in: a state in which the product is deeply embedded in existing systems and data structures, making migration to another service difficult. Examples: API integration with core systems, ID unification, audit logs, and meeting security/compliance requirements.

Network externalities: a state in which value increases the more people around the user adopt the product, making switching harder. Examples: Chatwork or Slack once collaboration with partners or other departments has become established.

Building lock-in and network-externality structures in advance creates a mechanism in which customers do not leave even after a price increase. Companies that see little churn after raising prices typically have well-designed switching costs.
Switching costs (スイッチングコスト), also framed as switching barriers (スイッチングバリア), are classified into procedural, financial, and relational types that raise the difficulty of changing providers.

Procedural switching costs include evaluation/uncertainty costs: the potential uncertainty that undesirable outcomes may occur when switching to an alternative about which the buyer has insufficient information.
Procedural switching costs include search and analysis costs: the time and effort required for exploration and analysis when deciding whether to switch.
Procedural switching costs include learning costs: the time and effort needed to fully master a new provider, including acquiring new skills and ways of working.
Procedural switching costs include setup/initiation costs: the time and effort required to start using a new service.

Financial switching costs include benefit-loss costs: forfeiting the economic advantages that accrue from continuing to use the current service (e.g., accumulated discounts, loyalty benefits, or volume terms).
Financial switching costs include monetary-loss costs: the one-time financial outlays incurred at the moment of switching.
Relational switching costs include personal-relationship loss: the emotional cost of breaking personal bonds formed with employees of the current provider.
Relational switching costs include brand/company-relationship loss: the emotional cost of breaking identification and personal bonds formed with the current provider’s brand or firm.

These categories of switching costs are a practical framework for understanding why B2B customers stay with an incumbent even after a competitor appears, and they are typically presented as a table mapping large categories (procedural / financial / relational) to specific cost types.

Smaregi implemented a rare 25% large-scale price revision for a SaaS company in 2023. Churn rose only 0.07 points quarter-over-quarter and actually fell 0.02 points on an annual basis, showing almost no impact from the hike. In the quarter of the increase, revenue grew +20.4% QoQ and +62.2% YoY at a roughly 4 billion yen scale—an exceptional growth rate that turned the price change into a strategic decision that structurally lifted the business.

kubell (Chatwork) has conducted gradual price revisions since 2021 while keeping churn stable and performance solid. The product is deeply embedded in business workflows and internal communication, intentionally raising switching costs and thereby supporting successful price increases.
Companies that succeed at raising prices share a common trait: they first build structural advantages that make price increases possible, rather than merely having the 'courage' to raise prices.

Pricing is value design. Price is the act of translating a company's offered value into market terms. It is not merely setting a rate card; it is the design work of defining and communicating the company's own value.

The key relationship for understanding price structure is WTP (customer's subjective willingness to pay / perceived value), P (the price the company sets), and C (the supplier's cost). Firms must design how much of the value they can capture within this three-way balance.

McKinsey analysis indicates that many companies fail to capture 30–50% of the value they should obtain. This 'value leakage' or missed capture is described as the biggest factor that stops growth. Pricing is the structural design work that closes this gap.
Pricing should start by accurately verbalizing what customers actually value (their perceived value), not by internal cost-plus or competitor-copying alone.
The classic 3C framework (Company / Competitor / Customer) is an effective starting point for pricing decisions.
Company (self): Define the profit level that must be secured by considering LTV, CAC, and gross-margin structure.
Competitor: Confirm relative positioning against substitutes and prevailing market price levels.
Customer: Grasp willingness-to-pay (WTP) both qualitatively and quantitatively as the customer's felt value.
Pricing's starting point is to harmonize internal needs (required profit) and market conditions (going rates) through the lens of customer value.
To raise price, first raise the customer's perceived value (WTP) itself rather than simply marking up.

Two complementary ways to amplify value: (1) Functional value improvement—make outcomes that directly hit customer KPIs (time saved, error reduction, revenue increase, etc.) visible; (2) Emotional/experiential value improvement—even with the same features, create 'reasons to choose with peace of mind' via brand, support quality, UI, SLA, etc.
When functional and emotional value are designed together as two wheels, price ceases to be 'something you raise' and becomes 'a reflection of updated value.'
Customer WTP is not uniform, so price diversity (packaging/structure) must be designed.
A practical structure is a good-better-best (Matsu-Take-Ume / pine-bamboo-plum) plan ladder that makes value stages explicit and thereby induces upgrades and cross-sells.
For mature companies, usage-based pricing is effective: charging according to customer value metrics such as usage volume, number of users, or data volume aligns usage with revenue.
The ideal pricing structure makes the customer's success experience itself become company revenue, as in HubSpot's contact-based billing.
When usage-based pricing is in place, development, customer success, and sales move on the same metrics, so organizational focus aligns naturally.
Pricing should be treated as culture, not a one-time decision: price must be continuously reviewed.
Build a culture of checking the balance between value and price through annual price reviews and value verification when new features are released.
A price increase should be communicated as sharing the evolution of value, not merely as a notification to customers.
If improvements and results are made visible to customers in ordinary times, price revisions are accepted as a natural conversation.
Strong companies treat price as management culture rather than as an event.
Pricing strategy is the last lever that determines company growth; designing price correctly can change the profit structure more fundamentally than launching a new product.
Price is a management intention that communicates the value the company provides to the market.
Companies that are not afraid to raise prices and can confidently assert value to customers advance to the next stage.
Pricing is a management practice of designing value and continuously drawing its trajectory in the form of price.
Multi-productization is not simply increasing the number of businesses; it is management design to redistribute the company's strengths and regain focus.

A growth ceiling arises from two limits at once: the time-axis limit of slowing customer-acquisition speed, and the structural limit of WTP (willingness to pay) as the upper amount a customer will pay for one problem.
The most realistic growth path after PMF in B2B is multi-productization (マルチプロダクト化), not jumping to entirely new markets.
Success starts from deepening the existing market: solving unsolved problems of existing customers, not from exploring new markets.

Two representative winning plays: (1) Cross-sell type — solve adjacent customer problems to stack LTV; (2) B-to-C shift type — use assets built in B2B (customers, data, channels, brand) as the base to expand value toward consumers.
Both plays design the next growth axis on existing strengths: customers, data, funnels/channels, and brand.

Once a company runs multiple businesses, the old organization no longer works. Sequence: integrated verification → independent PMF exploration → business-unit (divisional) structure. Decision rights, accountability, and evaluation must be updated by phase.
The founder/CEO must shift role from player to portfolio manager as the company multiplies products.

Sales design is binary and context-dependent: one-stop sales (customer-centric, all products) vs. specialized sales (expertise per product). The right choice is set by customer structure and business phase.
Whichever sales model is chosen, structural redesign is mandatory: CRM, evaluation systems, and lead-sharing rules must be rebuilt.
Pricing is the shortest lever to lift growth another notch. Price is the act of translating a 'value update' into the market; the ability to raise price is determined by structure, not courage.
Design switching costs (evaluation/learning/migration burden, economic loss, interpersonal and brand relationships), lock-in, and network externalities so that price increases are naturally accepted.
Fill the WTP–P–C gap (Willingness To Pay minus Price minus Cost). Companies that turn price updates from one-off 'events' into 'culture' are the ones that can stably draw a second growth curve.

Diagnostic questions that mark the starting line of the second growth period: Is the stall a customer-count ceiling or a WTP ceiling? Which adjacent problem of the same customers should the next (existing-market × new-product) offer solve? Where is the org on the integrated / independent / business-unit spectrum, and under what conditions will it migrate? Should sales unify the customer contact for cross-sell or win with product-level specialty? Are switching costs, lock-in, and network effects already designed if a price increase is needed? How will the company's strengths be reallocated across market, organization, sales, and price?

At ARR of 50億円 (~5 billion JPY), a B2B company can have strong market presence, healthy hiring and fundraising, and IPO within reach, yet still experience growth deceleration: numbers continue to rise but miss targets and the growth curve's acceleration flattens.

A typical executive meeting at this stage surfaces conflicting functional views: marketing reports that new contracts remain solid; finance warns that the domestic market is approaching its limit; sales argues that intense competition means the company can no longer win on feature differentiation; product emphasizes that customers now demand integrated rather than single-function offerings; alliances highlight that overseas majors have begun their offensive.
Reaching ARR 50億円 is itself a success marker, but domestic TAM analysis shows a ceiling is inevitable; remaining purely domestic makes exceeding 100億円 (~10 billion JPY) in revenue very difficult.
The competitive game itself is shifting from feature-by-feature competition to who controls the ecosystem.

Leadership conclusion at this inflection: domestic-market-only growth will hit a wall, so the company must seed the next growth engine, redefine the market, and have the resolve to move to the side that holds the initiative rather than remaining reactive.

In B2B growth (from PMF toward ¥10 billion in sales), reaching ARR of ¥5 billion can produce a sense of achievement while simultaneously making the ceiling of the domestic market clearly visible as a structural wall.
Key statement: Behind the sense of achievement of reaching ARR 50億円, the wall of the limits of the domestic market was beginning to become clearly visible.
After a SaaS company exceeds ARR of 5 billion yen, the first challenge it faces is not a product issue but the 'market ceiling' (市場の天井).
Even when expanding share within a category, growth rates gradually slow after a certain level; this is a structural phenomenon, not merely a sales or marketing execution problem.
SaaS businesses solve problems in a specific domain, so the TAM of that market always has an upper limit.
The Japanese market, as an island nation, tends to hit this TAM limit relatively earlier than overseas markets.
ARR of 5 billion yen is the point at which 'domain limits' (ドメインの限界) become visible as a management challenge.

In this phase many companies experience the sensation of 'anxiety despite growing' (伸びているのに焦りが生まれる): year-over-year sales and customer counts still rise, yet the slope of the growth curve flattens and former acceleration disappears.
Adding more salespeople or increasing marketing spend does not restore the previous growth rate.
The situation cannot be explained by looking at numbers alone.
The recommended breakthrough at this stage is to remake the market itself (市場をつくり替えることで突破する).
In later-stage BtoB SaaS growth (after PMF toward ¥10B revenue), the core strategic problem shifts from initial product-market fit to market redefinition and choosing which market to win in.
SaaS companies typically launch by specializing in one specific customer problem and grow rapidly by focusing on a narrow domain.
Japanese single-domain scale examples: SmartHR (HR/labor), Sansan (business-card management), Rakus (expense settlement), and freee (accounting); each scaled intensely within one domain.
Some firms have already crossed ¥10 billion in a single domain inside large industries, but those large industries are becoming saturated.
Future competition will confront the limit of a single domain sooner than in prior generations of SaaS.
The required response is to redefine the market the company fights in and expand into a broader market/domain definition.
Expansion choices relative to the current domain are horizontal expansion versus vertical integration (illustrated in Figure 6-1).
Key Japanese terms: 水平展開 (horizontal expansion) and 垂直統合 (vertical integration).
Horizontal expansion (水平展開) is a strategy of entering adjacent domains to capture new markets; SmartHR is a typical example (even post-¥10B, relevant earlier for companies aiming for that scale).

Early SmartHR dominated with a clear message of 'DX of labor management' (労務管理のDX): cloud-automating cumbersome social-insurance procedures for HR, eliminating paper and hanko—a theme that strongly resonated with Japanese companies at the time.

After capturing substantial TAM in the labor-management domain, SmartHR horizontally expanded from labor data into adjacent areas: talent management, HR evaluation, and payroll—not merely adding features but presenting a worldview of 'end-to-end management of all HR and labor affairs.'

This approach is not only 'spreading sideways' but 'integrating to amplify value': from labor affairs → overall HR → organizational data platform. Existing customer base and data assets are used to enter new categories, solve new customer problems, create new TAM, and gain synergy with the existing business. Horizontal expansion is a 'win with breadth' strategy.

Vertical integration (垂直統合) dominates the customer's business process from upstream to downstream, digging deep into the same value chain; common among vertical ventures. It can mean operating the business itself, not only providing the service (e.g., UniFa operating model kindergartens; atama plus operating cram schools).

Even after crossing the chasm, if adoption speed still does not rise fully, companies must show how operations and management improve with their product and what the world looks like when the product is fully utilized. Vertical integration is a 'win with depth' strategy.

Neither path is easy: vertical integration hits limits early if the domain is narrow (small market size caps growth no matter how deep you dig); horizontal expansion complicates development, sales, and CS and requires organizational redesign.

Both strategies require thinking through organizational design as part of strategy. Winning forever inside a single domain always has limits: even category-top share stops company growth if the market itself stops growing.
For companies past ¥5B in sales, the needed shift is from 'which market to fight in' to 'how to recreate the market.'
A prerequisite for either strategy is achieving first-recall (第1想起) within the category (e.g., SmartHR as the synonym for HR/labor SaaS).

Category expansion and brand recall: When discussing market expansion, the first companies recalled are those that have already built an overwhelming, dominant position in an existing category. A company that has not achieved first (top-of-mind) recall in its core category will only become a 'second-place' player no matter which other markets it enters.

Prerequisite for expansion strategy: An expansion strategy only begins to function after a company has first established itself as the top brand in its existing category. Without category leadership, adjacent-market moves fail to convert trust into adoption.

Brand dominance as expansion advantage: Firms that already dominate a category enjoy a structural advantage when expanding. Customers more readily accept new offerings because of existing brand trust. Example: If SmartHR (a Japanese HR SaaS leader) expands into performance evaluation or talent management, customers tend to accept the new service with the attitude 'If it is a SmartHR product, it is reliable.'

True meaning of category hegemony: Holding category hegemony is not merely about capturing market share. It is about dominating market psychology through brand recall—being the name that comes to mind first so that the brand itself shapes how the market thinks.

Path to breaking single-domain limits: To escape the ceiling of a single domain, a company must first seize hegemony in its existing category. Only then should it choose between vertical integration or horizontal expansion in order to increase customer touchpoints.
Ultimate strategic goal: The decisive objective is not simply to expand an existing market, but to remake (redefine/create) the market itself.
SaaS companies that have exceeded 5 billion yen in sales face one of their largest walls: the reality of 'suite-ification' (スイート化).
Single-domain growth has inherent limits; companies must create new TAM (Total Addressable Market) by incorporating adjacent domains.
Many companies that actually pursue suite-ification encounter far greater difficulties than they expected.
Suite-ification is not 'adding more features' but 'integrating structure.'
Structural integration intertwines multiple elements: technology, organization, culture, and customer experience.
Successful companies treat suite-ification as a core management theme and confront it head-on.
Failing companies treat suite-ification merely as an extension of development or sales work.
Suite-ification (スイート化) is never a smooth path: it requires technical integration, organizational integration, and consistency of customer experience. Many companies attempt it and stall midway.

Failed suite expansion example: a company that added too many products while expanding horizontally dispersed development resources; sales and CS stayed siloed per product so cross-sell stalled; customers perceived separate services rather than a suite, so they could not see suite value. Result: upsell rates fell and overall organizational efficiency worsened.
Suite-ification is not a ‘just add more products’ strategy. Without an overarching design philosophy that binds the whole together, it backfires.
The true purpose of suite-ification is to restructure the customer’s operations (顧客の業務を再構成する), not merely to assemble features.
SmartHR example: they framed the suite as ‘centralize HR data and use it for management’ (人事データを一元化し、経営に活かす). Redefining meaning for the customer is the actual value of a suite.
A suite succeeds only if it delivers concrete change such as: faster company-wide decision-making, unified data, or a stronger organization—not a mere collection of functions.
Successful suite companies achieve ‘redefinition of customer value’ (顧客価値の再定義).

Suite-ification is described as the most beautiful and most difficult strategy: beautiful because it is structurally sound (cross-functional problem solving, connecting data, maximizing LTV); difficult because every element of the company must be reconstructed.
Suite-ification is not mere new-business development. It is ‘an endeavor to redesign the company itself’ and ‘not category expansion but category redefinition’ (カテゴリの拡張ではなく、カテゴリの再定義).
Customers no longer choose by comparing features; they choose by which suite’s philosophy they empathize with.
Corporate hegemony (番権/覇権) is established not by technology or price but by domination of thought and structure. The reality of suite-ification most eloquently demonstrates this.
BtoB Growth Playbook addresses the five trials companies must overcome to grow from product-market fit (PMF) to 10 billion yen in sales.

A core strategic challenge is a approach that simultaneously possesses both beauty and difficulty; the degree of seriousness with which a company confronts this strategy determines whether it can acquire the next stage of rights or competitive position.
SaaS companies that have exceeded ¥5 billion in sales, while advancing suite-ification or market expansion, confront the reality that in-house development takes too long.

Even with an expanding customer base and a visible next growth area, launching a new product from scratch typically cannot be completed in 1–2 years; time spent acquiring technology, talent, and know-how allows competitors to fill the market.
Because time available for growth is finite, companies past ¥5 billion in sales should treat M&A as a means of “buying time.”
M&A is not merely a capital-policy tool; it is an initiative to expand the company’s own structure and create the next stage of growth.
In the suite-ification phase, acquiring and integrating products that cover peripheral functions or adjacent domains accelerates the increase in customer value.
Key framing: M&A buys time and, through post-merger integration, re-sets the value the company can deliver.
M&A (mergers and acquisitions) means more than buying new features, talent, or customers; it is an act of rewriting market structure around one's own company.

Pursuing product suite-ification through in-house development alone incurs enormous time and risk. M&A shortens that time by incorporating already market-validated products, technology, and talent and then integrating them.
For companies whose sales exceed 5 billion yen, M&A is an act of buying time and a form of leverage for structural expansion.
M&A is not a simple story of 'buy and you grow.' Its essence lies in post-merger integration (PMI).
An acquisition itself can be completed in a matter of months, but integration takes years. Neglecting PMI can produce organizational discord and even cause the company to lose speed.
The three critical elements of integration are: customer data integration, brand integration, and talent integration.
The essence of M&A is not incorporating another company into oneself, but changing oneself through another company.
For companies whose ARR exceeds 5 billion yen, M&A is shifting from a high-risk means to a necessary condition for growth.
As market speed rises and customer expectations diversify, the era of building everything in-house has ended.
Success versus failure is separated by whether a company has the philosophy of not merely buying, but integrating and redesigning value.
Once a SaaS company exceeds 5 billion yen in sales, the nature of its competitive battle becomes completely different from earlier stages.
In the early phase, a SaaS company could win with the value proposition of being more convenient, easier to use, and lower cost.
As enterprise adoption advances and the overall market matures, companies are no longer chosen solely on differences in features or price.
Customers are no longer selecting the 'product' itself; they are selecting the 'structure' (構造).
Structure encompasses decisions such as which platform to adopt, which ecosystem to connect with, and which brand to place trust in.
When the competitive arena (土俵) changes, SaaS companies enter a phase in which they are for the first time evaluated as 'structure designers' (構造の設計者).
In this phase, competition among SaaS companies themselves saturates, while 'competition between structures' (構造間の競争) surfaces—especially versus large SIers and versus overseas SaaS vendors.

Japan's B2B software market has historically been dominated by SIers (system integrators) and on-premise systems. Large-enterprise IT departments long outsourced work to specific SIers and accumulated years of customization, so business design, requirements definition, development, and operations were all handled by the SIer.

SaaS entered from outside this structure and offered new value: cloudification, standardization, and speed. Those advantages work until a SaaS company exceeds roughly ¥5 billion in revenue and must go deep into the enterprise market, where it collides head-on with the SIer structure.

At that stage, sales conversations change. Buyers say they intend to adopt but ask about integration with existing systems, or that they cannot easily switch functions because of their SIer relationship. Customer decision-making no longer completes with the SaaS product alone.

SIers are not mere competitors; they are part of the customer's decision-making process itself. The strategic question is how to enter the business flows the SIer already controls, or how to rewrite that structure.

Winning enterprise therefore requires redesigning the 'structure of introduction/implementation,' not just product quality. A common approach is to treat SIers as partners: do not make them enemies; make them allies, and reach customers the SaaS company cannot reach alone.

Collaboration is hard because the philosophies conflict: SaaS values standardization; SIers value customization. SaaS extensibility and API flexibility can look to an SIer like an uncontrollable, unstable element.

A key judgment is how far the SaaS company should internalize SIer-like work (onboarding, process design, data migration). Firms that pass ¥5 billion often expand onboarding teams and take on implementation and data migration themselves, moving from tool vendor toward SIer-like support.
To take hegemony, a SaaS company can no longer remain a 'tool vendor.' It must become a 'structure provider' that comprehensively offers business design, implementation support, and data integration.

A second shift is on the customer side: vendor selection is moving from IT departments toward business units and executives. The old 'leave it to the SIer and it is safe' model is weakening, creating an opening for SaaS if business departments can choose and drive adoption themselves.
SaaS companies should therefore redesign their sales structure around who actually makes the introduction decision, not around a default IT/SIer buying center.
When a customer's internal organizational structure changes, a SaaS provider's delivery structure must change as well.

Overseas enterprise giants (Salesforce, Microsoft, Workday, SAP) dominate with capital and brand; in Japan they already occupy a position where being chosen is the default, making it hard for local vendors to beat a 'global standard' even with a superior product.
The strategy Japanese SaaS firms should take is local specialization plus depth of customer relationships.

Sales and customer-success people who embed in the customer's organization and surface real field problems create 'relationship assets' that overseas giants cannot fully copy; closeness to the customer often matters more than a technology gap.
To seize market hegemony, SaaS companies need an ecosystem strategy: the era of a single self-contained product is over because customers compose operations from multiple SaaS tools.
Ease of integration with other SaaS becomes a decisive factor in adoption; building an ecosystem lets a product evolve from a service into an 'industry OS.'
Ecosystems rest on partner networks and communities; they are not only technical integrations but also industry-wide involvement and thought leadership.

As markets mature, customers decide by 'which company to trust.' In enterprise, brand acts as a passport at the start of a deal; heavy spend on TV and transit ads is often to satisfy the condition 'we don't contract with unknown firms,' i.e. to set the premise of a transaction rather than merely generate leads.
Hegemony is not excluding others but building a self-centered structure while involving other companies; winners construct ecosystem and brand as a set.

Once sales exceed about 5 billion yen, the question is which structure the company uses to hold the market: not feature superiority but structural design—internalizing SIer-like implementation and owning the customer's processes, creating an ecosystem that sets industry standards, or dominating market psychology via brand and awareness.
Mere tool vendors can no longer win; the watershed is whether the company can change the customer's decision-making structure itself.

After a SaaS company exceeds 5 billion yen in sales, the next challenge is that implementation proceeds but results do not materialize: new contract volume can keep growing while NRR plateaus, customers never master the product, usage stalls, and accounts that were 'implemented' never reach real operation and instead churn or downsell.
The structural mismatch is that sales can sell faster than customers can operationalize the product. This pattern repeats across industries.
Root causes include customer-side resource shortages, highly personalized (person-dependent) work structures, and the over-expectation that 'just implementing the tool will change everything.'

SaaS supplies tools, not transformation. In the Japanese market, the talent and culture needed to actually use those tools are often still underdeveloped, producing a growing stock of 'contracted but unused' and 'implemented but no outcomes' accounts that slows ARR accumulation.
The recommended response is a 'depth strategy' (深さの戦略): go inside the customer's operations and take ownership of results rather than stopping at the sale or the initial rollout.

Depth strategy (深さの戦略) for B2B SaaS: instead of widening the market via suite expansion or M&A, question how deeply the company can enter existing customers—go into the customer's field operations, redesign the business process itself, and build a structure that takes responsibility through to outcomes. This is the essence of BPaaS and in-house operation models.

Breadth vs depth: breadth expands the quantity of market handled (top-line growth); depth maximizes value per customer. Depth raises LTV, NRR, and switching costs. Short-term gross margin may fall, but the more the product is embedded in customer operations, the lower its substitutability, enabling long-term stable growth.
The next engine of SaaS growth is no longer new contracts but degree of penetration into customer operations (顧客業務への浸透度).

Depth strategy is a structural shift that evolves SaaS from mere tool provision into a results-provision business. BPaaS removes introduction friction; in-house operation demonstrates the ideal operational image; AI feeds that knowledge back into the product. Firms that close this loop unify customer outcomes with their own growth and create a structure that continuously increases LTV and NRR.

Most companies that exceed 10 billion yen in sales have established this 'depth structure.' BPaaS succeeds at introduction, in-house operation generates trust, and the resulting field knowledge and data evolve the product. The chain of depth is not only a growth strategy but has the power to transform industrial structure itself.
SaaS companies must change from supporting operations from the 'outside' to entering the 'inside' of those operations and jointly bearing result responsibility.

BPaaS (Business Process as a Service) combines SaaS delivery with operational support and commits to customer outcomes. Whereas SaaS assumed the customer's 'ability to use software,' BPaaS includes the 'ability to make it usable.'

BPaaS is especially important in the Japanese market because introduction staff typically juggle multiple concurrent duties and have little dedicated resource for system rollout or data preparation. If the vendor does not absorb initial introduction friction, the software's true value is never realized.

In the short term BPaaS is labor-intensive (introduction support, initial setup, daily operations proxy, etc.), so people-heavy work increases and gross margin declines; the trade-off is accepted for long-term embedding and lower substitutability.

In the education sector, atama plus rapidly grows as a SaaS providing AI teaching materials while also operating its own cram schools (juku) so it can itself manage the daily field where the AI materials are used.

Insights from self-operated sites—when instructors should rely on AI versus when human guidance is required, and which data collected in which way actually drive outcomes—are fed back into product improvement.
Self-operation is not merely a verification environment; it transcribes the SaaS design philosophy into actual operations, functioning as a learning loop.
Showing customers a live, self-operated site (as UniFa and atama plus do) produces immediate trust; an actually working model reduces psychological resistance to adoption far more than theory.
For a SaaS company, being able to say “we ourselves succeed in this form” is more persuasive than saying “if you do this you will succeed.” The self-operated model supplies that demonstration power.
Self-operation imposes heavy burdens (rising fixed costs, difficulty of maintaining field quality). Positioning it as R&D rather than a side business completely changes its meaning.

A self-operated field is a software company’s “laboratory” and an “observation device for redesigning reality.” Accumulated operational knowledge and data are recirculated into BPaaS or suite offerings. Once this cycle is established, the SaaS firm evolves from a mere tool vendor into an entity that redefines industry structure itself.

While advancing BPaaS or self-operation, M&A becomes a route to absorb operational knowledge and business know-how: acquiring BPO firms, implementation-support companies, or small field-close vendors and integrating product with operations. This is termed “depth M&A.”
The purpose of depth M&A is not revenue expansion but acquisition of operational knowledge (業務知).

In PMI, fusion of people and quality matters more than technology. Service SLA, field operational culture, and the “temperature” of customer contact must be preserved; disrupting them destroys acquisition synergy.
Successful acquirers do not fully absorb the target; they jointly create new operational standards while leveraging each side’s knowledge.
深さのM&A (depth M&A) is not an act of expanding the organization through acquisition; it is a management means of making one's own company one step more field-oriented (現場化).

深さの戦略 (depth strategy) short-term compresses profits: incorporating operational support raises personnel costs, and starting model operations inflates fixed costs. Firms still choose this path because they have designed management as covering gross-margin reduction with a recovery curve (粗利減を回収曲線で覆す).
BPaaS yields higher LTV and NRR, improved customer retention, and accumulation of field data that can dramatically raise product value in 2–3 years.

Typical depth-strategy sequence: provide generous support early and stack customer outcomes; standardization and automation then progress and human costs fall; insights gained from BPaaS are implemented inside the product, software accuracy rises, and gross margin recovers.
Depth strategy is the management decision to design in advance, and to accept, the pattern of short-term pain and mid-term recovery.

In investor dialogue, depth strategy is increasingly framed not as mere cost increase but as prepaid growth (成長の前払い). Clearly showing the period until LTV recovery maintains capital-market trust. Firms that can communicate that gross-margin decline is strategic succeed at balancing growth and efficiency.

Generative AI is currently the largest change agent in depth strategy. BPaaS and in-house field operations generate large volumes of unstructured work (report writing, data entry, inquiry handling, record summarization); many of these processes are entering automation or semi-automation.
AI in BPaaS fields does more than cut labor cost: it rapidly advances quality standardization. AI is used not to reduce people but to elevate human judgment to a higher order (人の判断を高次化する).

Example (atama plus in education): AI does not replace instructors; it increases the time instructors spend with each student. AI handles routine analysis and question generation so humans can concentrate on value judgment. This division of labor is the key to gross-margin improvement.

As AI adoption advances, BPaaS scalability rises sharply. AI learns past operational data and optimizes support for the next customer. The linkage of BPaaS and AI becomes a knowledge-production apparatus (知識の生産装置).
A virtuous cycle can be established in BPaaS in which operational/field data becomes training material for AI, and that AI in turn further streamlines BPaaS operations.
If that cycle is established, BPaaS evolves from a labor-cost-dependent model (人件費依存モデル) to a knowledge-asset-dependent model (知識資産依存モデル).
AI also supplies a new customer-value story: 'Our BPaaS continuously evolves because AI constantly learns from on-site/field data.' This narrative resonates with both investors and customers.
Changing BPaaS profit structure with AI while simultaneously refining brand and narrative will create a decisive difference in future 'depth strategy' (深さの戦略).
IPO (initial public offering) should be considered from the capital market's perspective as a way to pursue the next stage of growth, not merely as a fundraising event.
Once a company has grown to a certain scale, IPO comes into view and becomes a management theme for accelerating subsequent growth.
When the limits of the domestic market start to become visible, companies are expected to connect with capital markets and draw a new growth scenario.
IPO is not a goal; it is positioned as a 'social contract promising growth.'
Reorganization of the Tokyo Stock Exchange has tightened listing standards.
In the Growth market, a 'market capitalization 10 billion yen rule' was introduced; sustainable growth is valued more highly than mere sales scale.
Companies considering IPO at around 5 billion yen in sales will be asked by investors whether they can continue to maintain 30–40% growth.
If the growth rate falls below 20%, the company is regarded as a mature company.

For listed companies, declining profit margins lower valuation even when growth is being pursued; listed vs. unlisted status changes how companies are evaluated, so growth rate and profit margin must be skillfully balanced.

Investors do not look at growth rate alone. Efficiency metrics such as LTV/CAC, NRR (Net Revenue Retention), and churn rate are also heavily weighted. Companies with excessive sales investment face strict questioning about a path to profitability after listing.
IPO means entering a stage of transparency and accountability toward a new stakeholder: the capital market.

IPO benefits include higher name recognition; in enterprise markets, being a listed company itself functions as a trust signal. Hiring and fundraising become easier, and large moves such as M&A and overseas expansion become more feasible. IPO can be a catalyst that switches a company’s growth stage.

IPO constraints include quarterly disclosure that intensifies short-term performance pressure and the need to balance growth vs. profit. Profit-focused investor attitudes constrain firms that want to remain in an investment phase. Governance and internal-control requirements reduce management freedom but also strengthen organizational capability.
Valuation is decided by whether a realistic growth path can be shown—not by market size or vision alone. Listing without adequate preparation destroys trust and constrains long-term growth.

IPO is a waypoint, not a goal. Whether funds are used to build a growth foundation or the brand is strengthened for the next stage, the real contest is whether sustainable growth can be designed after listing.
For SaaS companies that have exceeded ARR of 5 billion yen, IPO is an unavoidable trial. The ability to design growth together with the capital market determines subsequent market position.

Sales of 5 billion yen is both a milestone and a turning point for SaaS companies. The structure that supported single-domain growth hits its limit: market ceilings become visible and the nature of competition changes.
Beyond this point, merely building a good product is not enough to win. Companies must redesign the business structure itself and construct a new structure capable of capturing market dominance.
In mature B2B SaaS markets, competition is a battle over structure rather than feature comparison. Customers no longer choose which tool to introduce; they choose which mechanism or system to ride.
A SaaS company's real competitors are not neighboring startups but the customer's internal organizational structure and the industry's overall operating mechanisms themselves.

Polishing the product without understanding this structure will eventually halt growth. Companies that can change structure can redefine the market and enter a growth trajectory exceeding 10 billion yen (ARR).

In this phase the keys are suite-ification (スイート化) and acquiring hegemony. Suite-ification is a high-difficulty strategy: integrating multiple products around customer data to optimize entire operations and redesign the customer's business structure as a management challenge.
M&A functions as an accelerator, not a mere complement to suite-ification. It is a management act to buy missing functions, talent, and customer bases, then integrate them to create a new structure.

These structural changes are supported by brand and a trust relationship with capital markets. As markets mature, evaluation shifts from growth rate to sustainability of structure. Simply growing ARR does not satisfy capital markets; they want to know on what structure growth rests and which market the company intends to dominate.
IPO is the company's answer to society on those questions. Capital markets coldly assess whether the structure built through suite-ification and M&A can continuously generate value.

Hegemonic companies do not treat these as separate initiatives. They recognize the limits of a single domain, build an ecosystem, amplify customer value via suite-ification, expand structure via M&A, and support it with brand and capital. Only companies that consistently design and execute structure cross the 10-billion-yen ARR wall.
Markets are not too small to grow; companies fail to grow because they do not try to change structure.

Strategic choice for a company: continue competing via single-domain expansion, create a domination structure through suite-ification, buy time via M&A, or redefine the industry itself while involving brand and capital markets.

For B2B companies that have exceeded ARR of 5 billion yen, the greatest risk is not deciding which structure they will use to seize market hegemony; every structural choice is difficult, but indecision is worse.
Companies that exceed ARR of 10 billion yen are not merely companies that kept growing; they are companies that continuously rebuilt and replaced their structures.
A company should ask whether it is designing the next market structure or still fighting inside a structure it created in the past.
The path to hegemony always belongs to those who draw (design) the structure, not those who only compete within an existing one.
This closing argument sits in a BtoB growth playbook covering the path from PMF (product-market fit) to 10 billion yen in sales and the five trials companies must overcome on that path.

Reaching 10 billion yen in sales is an extremely high and steep path for Japanese B2B startups and new businesses; the authors tried to logically verbalize and systematize the route to that summit using the concept of five walls (5つの壁).
In practice, building a 10 billion yen business involves many unexpected hard things (ハードシングス): people and organization problems, major external-environment changes, and internal/external troubles.
Large growth is realized only through the accumulation of facing each difficulty head-on without running away and continuously making strict decisions.
The playbook was written to support the lonely battles of those challengers and to deliver practical weapons that help them push through the walls.

Field work is not a smart world solvable by beautiful logic alone: it means wrestling with questions that have no correct answers, getting muddy, and fighting alongside executives and business leaders.

The authors’ venture-support team (リブ・コンサルティング) has accompanied 100+ companies across 500+ projects on GTM strategy, sales-mechanism building, and launching enterprise sales and partner sales, aiming to be partners/comrades (パートナー・戦友) who share growing pains rather than mere consultants.
